subtopic: MR. MACQUARRIE    ANNIVERSARY OF CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
MR. MACQUARRIE    ANNIVERSARY OF CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct the attention of the house to an event of national importance and historic significance which occurred in my constituency. Exactly 100 years ago, at two o'clock in the afternoon of September 1, 1864, the Charlottetown conference was called into session in the legislative council chamber of Prince Edward Island. Later that afternoon the official delegates from the maritime provinces agreeably and readily opened the conference doors to their fellow legislators from Canada and, by setting aside the smaller plan of maritime union and discussing a greater federal union instead, the conference delegates of 1864 laid the foundations of the great and free dominion whose people we collectively represent in this chamber.
As with other gatherings, Mr. Speaker, before and since, the Charlottetown conference illustrated that many human endeavours begun poorly may end brilliantly. Delegates from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were not met by their island hosts, and there was not sufficient hotel space for the Canadians. Not surprisingly, the Prince Edward Island government was criticized by the press for its inept and inhospitable performance. But again, not surprisingly, the government had its explanations; the Nova Scotia delegation arrived earlier than expected, the New Bruns-wickers later and the Canadians in greater numbers than had been anticipated. Happily, history records that these little slips were soon quite overborne by the lavish hospitality which the islanders in succeeding days extended to their visitors.
Many at the time were unimpressed, Mr. Speaker, by the actions and utterances of the politicians of 1864, but others more perceptive appreciated more fully what was taking place in their time. The Charlottetown Monitor viewed the conference as "perhaps the most important event-as far at least as
the future destinies of these colonies are concerned-that has occurred during the present century". It hoped that the delegates' deliberations would "culminate in the creation ... of a great nation in this western hemisphere of which neither we nor our remotest posterity will ever have cause to be ashamed".
May we today, Mr. Speaker, as we honour the fathers of our nation, drawing strength from their devotion, inspiration from their accomplishment, and example from their performance, go on to preserve that which they bequeathed us. Of them it was later declared, "Providence being their guide they builded better than they knew". Of us may it be said "They destroyed not what their fathers left them, rather did they ever cherish, strengthen and extend the nation which faith had conceived and wisdom constructed".
As one of the representatives of the cradle of confederation, Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity of saying these few words, inadequate as they are in relation to the magnitude of the event they are intended to honour.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Acting Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. MACQUARRIE    ANNIVERSARY OF CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught), I should like to echo the words of the hon. member for Queens, my fellow academic, and I will not in the least attempt to differ with him about the historical view he has given to the house this afternoon. Indeed, the hon. gentleman is a lily I would not attempt to gild. But it did occur to me, sir, that since at Charlottetown a meeting is taking place to commemorate that original meeting of the founding fathers which, whatever the welcome may have been at the beginning, seemed to be very hospitable before the close if one can judge from the accounts of the food and other dainties which were consumed at the time, I doubt whether these latter day statesmen would have as strong stomachs as the original Fathers of Confederation, though I am sure they have just as strong hearts.
I do think, sir, that on this day we should look forward to even greater development
7514	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry than we have seen in that century that has
passed.
It did occur to me, sir, that the house might wish to have the opening address which is being made in Charlottetown today by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister added not in the record but as an appendix to the record in commemoration of this day- a day, I might add, very much happier than that day a quarter of a century ago that all of us remember when that terrible war started from which the world is still recovering.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Forestry. It has to do with the serious agricultural situation, particularly in the province of Quebec. I would ask him what he meant when in a speech at Ste Lucie, Quebec, he is reported, as found in Le Soleil, to have made this statement:
Mr. Sauve explained to a couple of hundred farmers that the task would be difficult-
That is the task of bringing ARDA into full and factual achievement.
-once the new program was put into effect because "at that moment the game of politics will come into the picture".
What did the minister have in mind in that regard, and what are the difficulties he anticipated by the use of those words?

Mr. Speaker, at that time I was not referring to ARDA but to the problems of eastern agriculture and the new outlook that would be necessary to solve those problems; that would 

be very difficult political decisions to be taken by all parties concerned, provincial and federal, and that there would be political opposition to some of the proposals which would be made because some people might benefit from contrary views for political ends. I have not in mind any particular party or people, just the straight game of politics as we know it in the provinces.

What were the particular proposals the minister had in mind as he placed them before this gathering, and what particular political interference would there be in the application of such a non-political plan as the one which was set up under the distinguished leadership of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle?

I was not referring to ARDA but to the problems of eastern agriculture, as mentioned in the eastern farm survey which was tabled in the house about two months ago. All the problems were mentioned in this report; I brought it to the attention of the people. We were discussing the general situation of eastern agriculture. I was not speaking of ARDA. I did not divulge any of the proposals we intend to make to the provinces for the renewal of the agreements.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Forestry.
In establishing his farm program for eastern Canada, does he propose to take into account the political consideration to which he referred in his speech?

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that extremely serious problems will have to be worked out when the federal and provincial governments advance proposals to find a solution to the farm problem of eastern Canada.
When we have proposed those solutions to the people, there will undoubtedly be some who will have opposite views, which is entirely normal. Never in the statements I made in Ste Lucie de Beauregard did I talk about anything except the normal game of politics. I have not seen the report or newspaper clipping which the Leader of the Opposition holds in his hand, but I am sure that I did not say anything wrong there.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. A few moments ago, if I am not

mistaken, the Minister of Forestry said: Politics as we know it in the province of Quebec.
Could the minister tell us-
No.

When reading over your
blues, you will find those words at the end of your first reply to the Leader of the Opposition. You said: "As we know it in the province of Quebec."
Does the minister mean by this that such a situation only exists in the province of Quebec?
I never said that, Mr. Speaker. [Text]

have a supplementary question for the Minister of Forestry. Is the minister undertaking an unusual recruitment drive for technical personnel in view of the expected expansion of the activities of his department?
No, we are dealing through the civil service commission in the normal way.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Forestry.
Could he tell us if one of the decisions he is supposed to take in co-operation with the Quebec government and which, as he put it, might not be a popular one is consistent with the rumour now going around to the effect that the federal government and the Quebec provincial government would be advising a fairly large number of farmers to leave their farms and go into some other industrial fields?

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING MEMBERS AND STAFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would direct a question to the Acting Prime Minister. It has to do with sordid and, if I may use language within the restrictions of parliament, scurrilous statements made by one Macdonald which cast aspersions on all members of

Inquiries of the Ministry this house who were members in 1961, as well as on the staff of parliament. This was a general allegation that was made. Believing in freedom of speech as I do, and as I know the hon. gentleman does, is it the opinion of the government that the allegations that have been made constitute a disparagement of the House of Commons and its members and a contempt of this house?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Acting Prime Minister):
maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING MEMBERS AND STAFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I imagine that I read the same press report of these utterances as the right hon. gentleman. I read it immediately before coming into the house and have had no chance at all of discussion with any of my colleagues. Moreover, it is well known that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice are absent in Charlottetown. It would not have been possible therefore, I think, for the government to form any opinion on this matter.
I must say, speaking as a member of parliament, that I think it is a perfectly shocking kind of allegation to appear, and quite frankly I am most reluctant to believe that it has any kind of substance whatsoever. When we think of what was said by this same person about Hon. M. J. Coldwell, which was refuted completely yesterday, I think his credibility as a witness has been somewhat discredited already. However, I do think it is a matter on which it would not be the government but the law officers of the crown that would form an opinion as to whether any kind of appropriate action could be taken which would not in any way endanger the right to speak foolishly and recklessly, which is one of the prized possessions of free people.

maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING MEMBERS AND STAFF
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the summation on the part of the Acting Prime Minister is an excellent epitome of freedom; but freedom does not, of course, include the right to libel in general or in such a way as actually to cast a shadow on all the members of this house and on all the staff of this house who have been here since 1961. Personally I am not concerned about contemptible statements of this kind, but I do think the minister should bring this matter before the Prime Minister, and any decision made by the Prime Minister in his position as custodian of the rights and prerogatives of parliament will, I am sure, be in the best interests of us all.

maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING MEMBERS AND STAFF
speechtext:
I quite agree with the right hon. gentleman. I would go further and say that I believe the only way in which there should be any abridgment of freedom

of speech is by the rule of law; and while this house is frequently referred to as a court, it is not a court in that sense. The only proper place for the adjudication of questions as to whether freedom of speech has turned into offensive licence is in the law courts of our country, and I hope no decision of that kind will ever be made anywhere else.

maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING MEMBERS AND STAFF
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the implications of this to all members, may I ask which member of this House of Commons is going to take the matter to a court of law?

maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT RESPECTING MEMBERS AND STAFF
speechtext:

The house resumed, from Monday, August 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially

as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.

Mr. Speaker, at 10.30 last night when the house adjourned I was speaking in support of the subamendment to the amendment to the flag resolution, and had not quite completed my remarks.
At the conclusion of my remarks last night I was urging all hon. members to lend their support to the subamendment. I strongly urge some member of the government to rise in his or her place and indicate the government's support for the subamendment, for if someone did this we could immediately move on to other urgent business. However, on reading Mr. Newman's article in the Toronto Star yesterday it would appear that the government has no legislation ready. Under the subheading "No Bills Ready" Mr. Newman says:
The Conservatives' (filibuster has not, as is generally believed, prevented parliament from dealing with a backlog of essential legislation. The Liberal administration, unaccountably, has no major bills ready for debate. The pension plan, which was supposed to be the showpiece of the Liberal's first year in office, is now in its fourth sad mutation.
It does seem inexcusable that the government has no legislation ready. It is further proof of a mismanaged and badly organized session. The Prime Minister and the government house leader have to take full responsibility for this. The order of business is in their hands. The Minister of Justice entered the debate last Thursday when he suggested the extension of the hours of sitting. This shows a lack of understanding of the situation.
This is the 139th day of this session and so far there has been no recess. I urge that some consideration should be given to the welfare of the staff. I merely wish to point out that the Hansard reporters, the Hansard staff generally and others are working under pressure and against time. If orderly recesses were arranged it would be much better for everyone concerned. This is another indication of the mismanagement of this session.
Our Indian citizens have not been consulted about the flag. Their wishes have not been taken into consideration. The Indians

do not like a flag which does not contain the union jack. They are afraid that removal of the union jack would mean that the treaties they have made with the Queen would also be done away with. Anything which gives rise to fears or suspicion in the minds of people should be avoided.
The only logical and reasonable approach to this issue is the holding of a referendum. Many members have stressed the need for unity, and have pointed out that a flag should unite people. There is no point in changing the present flag until our people plainly want a new one and until there is an agreement among the majority on a design. If such a flag, when selected, would tend to bring about a greater degree of unity, then it would serve a useful purpose. The present proposed flag does neither of these things.
If the Prime Minister believes that the flag proposed in this resolution would bring about unity and respect, then I suggest he accept the subamendment forthwith and pass the matter on to the people for their consideration. I have faith in the tolerance and understanding of the people of Canada.
I believe that any decision they themselves make will help the ties that bind and result in a stronger and more united Canada. I personally want to see a free, strong and united Canada. There is no room for dictatorship or dictatorial methods in our society. Let us forthwith pass this issue over to the people for them to make a decision. Then parliament can move forward and take action on the many important pieces of legislation which should be dealt with and which affect the economic well-being of every Canadian.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was impressed at the opening of this sitting when the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) and the Minister of Transport, as Acting Prime Minister, recalled the days of 100 years ago when we saw the beginning of the action which culminated in the British North America Act and brought about the uniting of Canada with Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
It is well to recall the events of those days at a time when we are discussing a matter of great importance to Canada, to her people, to her destiny, and above all to her unity now. And it is well to recall the difficulties of those days for many, especially for the faint hearted. The position was one of defeatism. There were separatists in those days, too. There were annexationists who believed 20220-476
Canadian Flag
that the ultimate destiny of Canada was to join the United States. Indeed, as the house very well knows, from 1776 under the articles of confederation Canada had the right and the prerogative to join the 13 colonies on an equal basis on the terms under which they entered their journey into history as the United States of America.
One of the matters dealt with during this conference in Charlottetown might well have been consideration of a general agreement by the premiers of the provinces and the Prime Minister of Canada on designs, or on a design, for a national flag for Canada.
Hear, hear.

However, that was not to be; for the Prime Minister had seen fit months ago to determine his design and to determine, as well, that parliament should accept that design or face an election. It took three months for the Prime Minister to realize that the bludgeon, the threat, would have no effect on Her Majesty's loyal opposition. When he found that to be the case he decided he would in fact grant a free vote.
The Prime Minister and the premiers are meeting. I hope they will be able to achieve the repatriation of the constitution. We almost succeeded and would have done so but for one or two comparatively minor matters to which objection was taken by the province of Quebec and, even more so, by the province of Saskatchewan when that province was under a socialist government. Now there has been a change. It is not for me to discuss the merits or demerits of that change, but there has also been a change in the premiership, and the new premier has agreed that action may be taken. So we may hope that after the many failures of the past we shall attain now, with the assistance of the tremendous contribution made by the minister of justice in my administration, that which has eluded Canadians for many, many years.
It is well to recall the speeches of 1864 and 1865. Some today talk about Canada being two nations. That did not represent the views of John A. Macdonald or Georges Etienne Cartier. It does not represent the views of two members of the cabinet today. The Minister of Forestry has come out foursquare for one Canada, and the Minister without Portfolio has stated that he believes this is one nation and not two. Also I recall that another member of the cabinet, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, ridiculed the view I expressed of one Canada and said it was nothing but a futile slogan; but in the intervening months

Canadian Flag
two members of the cabinet have broken with the views of other members of the cabinet in this regard, and it is worthy of note that they are both from the province of Quebec. Indeed, they represent the views of Macdonald.
I quote Macdonald's words in 1865 at the third session of the provincial parliament of Canada:
-it seems to me as to them, and I think it will so appear to the people of this country, that, if we wish to be a great people; if we wish to form-using the expression which was sneered at the other evening-a great nationality, commanding the respect of the world, able to hold our own against all opponents, and to defend these institutions we prize; if we wish to have one system of government, and to establish a commercial union... obeying the same sovereign, owing the same allegiance. ... if we wish to be able to afford to each other the means of mutual defence. .. .this can only be obtained by a union of some kind between the scattered and weak boundaries composing the British North American provinces.
I suggest that hon. members also read the speech of Cartier, the embodiment of French Canada and its aspirations, made on February 7, 1865. He dealt with the discussions that had taken place:
The matter resolved itself into this, either we must obtain British North American confederation or be absorbed in an American confederation. Some entertained the opinion that it was unnecessary to have British North American confederation to prevent absorption into the vortex of American confederation. Such parties were mistaken. We knew the policy of England towards us-that she was determined to help and support us in any struggle with our neighbours.
Those days and those fears of course no longer exist. Then he went on to say:
The absorption of this province into the United States had long been contemplated, as would be seen from the 7th article in the original draft of the constitution (American).
Then he referred to article 7, which ends up with these words:
But, except Canada, no other colony shall be admitted into the confederacy without the assent of 11 or more votes, as the case may require, by the confederation being extended.
Then he said:
As early as 1775, the French Canadians were solemnly addressed in a proclamation by General Washington, who called upon them to abandon the flag of their new masters, inasmuch as they could not expect anything from those who differ from them in language, in religion, in race, and in sympathies. But what was the conduct of the French Canadian people under these circumstances -what was the attitude of the clergy and the seigneurs? It was the right in treating this chapter of our history, to render justice to whom justice was due and it was truth to say that the seigneurs, forming as they did, the educated class of our

population at that early epoch, had fully understood that the object and aim of those who appealed to them was the downfall of the monarchical system in America.
Then he went on to say-and these are not his words, they are mine-they had not been moved. Then he said:
Incited by these motives, and encouraged by the advice of many friends of liberty among you, the grand American congress have sent an army into your province-
Then he dealt with the reaction of those who but a few years before had found themselves in the position of having lost. They joined; they stood. Then he said this:
The question for us to ask ourselves was this: Shall we be content to maintain a mere provincial existence, when, by combining together we could become a great nation... a great nation could not be formed-
-unless there was a joining with Lower Canada-
-in great part French and Roman Catholic, and Upper Canada.. .English and Protestant-
-the other provinces mixed.
That was their aim. That was their purpose. That was their dream, and I think that purpose and that objective are as true today as when they were uttered by the Macdonalds and the Cartiers, repeated by the Lauriers and the St. Laurents and by the Lapointes throughout the years of Canadian parliamentary life.
Today I am going to review something of the elements that have been brought before this house so powerfully by so many members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition in recent weeks. I read in the press, I hear from the voices of those who see nothing good in any stand the Conservative party takes, criticism of parliament today and criticism of the speeches made. I hear the strident voices of criticism saying the speeches have been boring. No one can say I participated except for 25 minutes, so I have been a listener; and I say to you, sir, that in almost a quarter of a century of membership in the House of Commons I have not seen or heard more consistently good speeches than have been delivered here, coming as they were from the heart, coming from the soul, and coming from the feelings and traditions that we support.
Hear, hear.
Oh, oh.

I am not talking about hon. gentlemen opposite. Their contribution has been the contribution of the hon. member for Lotbiniere, who has led them. No longer

is he to be with us, Mr. Speaker. The voice of interruption is to be stilled. For the last two weeks he has been rotating from seat to seat, apparently representing a new leadership on the government side, because certainly they have not shown other leadership in this regard. They have been silent. Why, the silence of the sepulcher does not exceed the silence of a government under attack.
And do you know why they are silent? Well, hon. gentlemen sometimes reveal the reasons they are silent when they speak outside the house. The hon. member for Port Arthur has a program on television, and he has been able to mobilize hon. gentlemen from all parts of the house. I regard it as a most interesting program, "Fisher's Frolics," and I do not say that disrespectfully because I say that he is able to draw out-I think the expression is "draw out"-the truth, by that bedside manner he exhibits.
It is amazing what he has been able to achieve. Do you know why they are silent, Mr. Speaker? I am not going to read it all, but if any hon. gentleman would like it tabled I would be glad to do so. He had an interview with two Liberal members on August 2, and he started out by saying of them:
Neither in my opinion is a rubber stamp-
In other words "there are no rubber stamps here." They gave their experience. They talked of these great men who occupy the front seats of Liberalism. They spoke of it, and what did they say? They seemed to detect an attitude of domination. They believed these great men should have their say. Let me quote one hon. member.
Name?

He said "They have a special place". He was referring to ministers:
It was said, I won't say where it was said, I'll say very recently it was said by a minister to a backbencher, "You are not the same as we are".
Oh, oh.
The typical attitude.

"You backbenchers, you are made of other stuff. In fact", said the hon. member-these are the very words he used-"How dare you say you are the same as we are?" The hon. member occupies a prominent place in the ranks of Liberalism opposite. Then another spoke and he said in effect, "Well, we don't know what is happening. We never know what is going to take place. They don't tell us anything". Then he said:

Our people are amazed when an order is issued and they will call you up and say to you you know about these new wharfage charges. No, I don't know anything about them. Yet they could defeat me, but somebody initiated them that even the minister doesn't know too much about.
There is where he touched a tender nerve. Perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite would like me to read some more. Even the Minister of National Defence is mentioned. This Liberal member said, in effect, that the minister could not trust them:
He didn't even trust it to be typed by the establishment.
The minister had to make his notes in his own handwriting, otherwise he might have been overwhelmed. Then he said:
I know how people tick and this is the trouble in Ottawa.
One of them said the trouble in Ottawa is that they don't know what is happening. Mr. Speaker, now you are beginning to see why it is these people are silent. They are strong, silent men who make their observations from a seated position because they are afraid to stand up.
Sir, never have I seen anything approaching the attitude of this government. Only one minister apart from the Prime Minister has spoken. The Minister of Justice has made two general observations. Why is this, sir? These two members to whom I have alluded, who bared their souls to the Canadian people on television, who opened the secret recesses of their innermost depths, say "We don't know anything about these things because we belong to a different category". That is why they are not speaking. Two of them spoke, the hon. member for York-Humber and the hon. member for York East; and what they said was tremendously revealing. It indicated that nobody knew anything about what was going to be brought forward.
I am now going to deal with the course that was taken by the Prime Minister. I am going to be very restrained in my observations regarding him today, in his absence, because there will be other opportunities, I am told, for me to speak before this matter is concluded.
Hear, hear.

We would like to know, not what the private members had to say; not the digits referred to by the two hon. members, but who were the four English speaking ministers who sold the Prime Minister on this flag design. There is one of the great mysteries. Mr. Stewart of the Montreal Star said over the C.B.C. that this

Canadian Flag
was so. Who were they? I do not want to embarrass anyone, but the information I have is that two of them come from Toronto and one from the Pacific coast. I immediately absolve the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I designate the Postmaster General, because he came up with the three maple leaves on a stamp. I am going to deal with that, because what he said in April was different from what he said last week in this regard.
Who were these four? Why don't we get this information? These men deserve to have their names perpetuated in the annals of parliament. They showed the Prime Minister something that he never showed to his members until after he had revealed it at a siesta at 24 Sussex drive. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that he placed this design over the fireplace and said "I hanker after it". On the basis of recent experience he is hankering after something else at the moment.
A handkerchief.

The Prime Minister said he hankered after it. These members had it given to him, and they cannot defend it. That is why they are silent. Why was this matter rushed before the house? What happened? To whom did the Prime Minister make promises? We don't know. In the month of February there was no reference to this matter in the speech from the throne; several weeks later there was no reference to it among the priorities.
Mackenzie King knew what a matter like this would do to the unity of this country. The Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent knew what would happen. Why was this matter suddenly brought forward? Never at any time in the election campaign had the Prime Minister said that by a distinctive flag he meant one from which was removed the union jack. There was not a word about that. That impression was left in the province of Quebec, but not by the Prime Minister. In other parts of Canada it did not appear in the program or in the advertisements, and I have them here. There is not one word. This parliament has no mandate and this government has no mandate to do what they are trying to do.
I am going to deal, Mr. Speaker, with some of the frenzied fantasies of the press and radio in their criticisms of the Conservative party for the stand they have taken. For who else is going to stand with us? Is it going to be the hon. gentlemen of the New Demo-

cratic party? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on January 12, 1964 advised the Legion in Manitoba that he was for the red ensign. He has changed; a metamorphosis has come over him in recent months. Will we get from that party the support of any more than two, three or four members in this regard?
Let us vote and you will find out.
What about the Social Credit party? We have yet to find out where they stand, with the exception of one or two members. We want to know.
Let us vote.

Ah, they say let us vote. Mr. Speaker, that illustrates above everything else the philosophy of the people who have said that. That is what they say under alien forms of government, just "vote". We know where the Creditistes stand. I look at my hon. friend the Minister without Portfolio and recall some of his statements regarding the leaders of the Social Credit party and the Creditistes. It must be the words of love and affection he spoke which now bind them to the bosom of Liberalism.
Are you jealous?

May I point out this fact. There are matters of immediate consequence on which action is needed. For example, what about the economic situation of which the Minister of Finance speaks so blandly? What about the pension legislation? We had an explanation of that when the question was asked, "Have you got it ready? If so, put it on". Why do not the government bring in that legislation? Are they changing their minds again for the third time?
The fourth.

For the fourth time.
Where is the legislation promised by the Minister of Agriculture. This is legislation which is going to bring about a new heaven and new earth agriculturally. Where is this legislation? We are not holding up anything, and hon. members opposite have not anything to hold up except themselves. There is not one iota of truth in the suggestion that we are holding anything up. We are holding up-
A vacation.
Oh, oh.

I would say to my hon. friends opposite that all of them have qualifications for drama in an animal field. What

are we holding up? We are holding up the government-
Right.

-on behalf of millions of Canadians. We are putting up a meaningful fight for a meaningful flag for Canada. We have said, and I repeat, in the addresses given by hon. gentleman in this party that we have always stood for a distinctive flag; but never at any time did the Conservative party, any more than the Liberal party, openly contend for anything other than a flag which was called distinctive by Mackenzie King and by Louis St. Laurent. Do you know where they made their mistake? They let their sycophants believe there would be a token fight and they would push this thing through and achieve what the Prime Minister wants as a personal flag.
The hon. member for York East revealed something that must be of interest to hon. members in various parts of Ontario and elsewhere when he said "We did not expect that there would be such a strong feeling on the part of Canadians". Mr. Speaker, Gallup polls cannot convey the soulful things of life. Where would Canada be today so far as the flag is concerned if it were not for the fight put up by this party standing alone?
I intend, sir, to call the great parliamentarians of the past to give their views as to a government endeavouring to push through something that the people generally do not want. They have played with parliament. They want the people to believe that all this legislation which they have in their minds but which they have not been able to translate into legislative form would be brought in if only we abdicated our responsibilities. They misconstrued the attitude of the people.
A few weeks ago the government were talking about an election. They said that was the reason we were fighting. We have made it perfectly clear that this is not so, because this is not the kind of issue upon which a general election should take place. But that is what they said. Today the Minister of Transport said in effect that the achievement of freedom demands the right of free speech. He is one of those to whom the press and radio have been most free in their free speech, and they have never heard me take a stand against it.
I ask, and parliament has the right to ask, that both sides be given not an expurgated edition, not a translated interpretation,
Canadian Flag
but actually the other side of the equation. We have not been able to get that so far, but someone has stated that the stand we are taking is getting through to the people. I do not know how it is getting through, but whereas three weeks ago there was criticism, more and more the attitude in every province, including the province of Quebec, indicates that the importance of this debate is finding its way through.
Mr. Speaker, they have been assisted by one United States magazine that masquerades in Canada as Canadian, but which week after week reveals one side of the equation. We have had our experience in the past, in 1962 and 1963, with extraterritorial interference. Let me interpolate here. There is an election campaign now on in the United States. Canadians should use that same discretion regarding an election in that country as we ask from them for Canada.
It has been argued that Canada does not have a distinctive flag. She had one, as was said in parliament by Mr. Ilsley, now the chief justice of Nova Scotia. The red ensign flying over parliament from 1867 to 1904; the red ensign was declared to be the flag for the army overseas in 1943; the red ensign was declared in 1945, until parliament otherwise directed, to be Canada's national flag. I have heard some say "But think of it; the Prime Minister brought this matter before parliament rather than doing it by order in council". Mr. Speaker, he could not do it by order in council, because that order in council of 1945 stated explicitly that a change could only be made by parliament.
Sir, I summarize these few general remarks I have made by referring to an article by Guy Lamarche in magazine Maclean's, September edition. Mr. Lamarche was speaking of our country and, reading from the translation, he said:
Here, we deliberately chose to adopt a national flag under the worst possible conditions...
Not only should we have waited, but it should have been orchestrated and executed with brio as an important step in our adolescence.
It was a question of public relations and I cannot understand how the image makers of Mr. Pearson, who work so hard to make us swallow their productions, were unable to convince the Prime Minister that at least in the matter of the flag, the public interest demanded that they should be allowed to make a success of it...
Instead of this, they spent their time saying the flag was a question full of sentiment and emotion, going right to the heart of every Canadian: and then nothing at all was done to reach the heart and sentiment of these Canadians...
Mr. Speaker, we have nothing to apologize for or explain in respect of the stand we

Canadian Flag
have taken. This is not a frivolous or captious stand. This is a stand based on abiding principles. I say this to you, and through you to the government. We in Her Majesty's loyal opposition are here to all intents and purposes standing alone in this house, but we do not represent a small minority of the Canadian people. Sir, we have a responsibility, and the government tries to becloud the issue by saying they have got legislation ready. Mr. Speaker, no arteries of legislation are being stopped when the government has no legislative items ready. We have passed all the legislation that has been brought before parliament-
What about redistribution?

-except redistribution. Everything has received consideration, and the only reason redistribution was not passed is because the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre decided he wanted to change the ideas of the government regarding appointments being made, one by the prime minister and one by the leader of the opposition. There was also a question raised as to the relative tolerance that should exist as between urban and rural areas. We showed signs of being able to come to an agreement. We suggested 20 per cent was too low. What about Mr. Lesage in the province of Quebec; what did he do? He raised this to 25 per cent in his province, according to the press.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would permit me to ask him a question.
Yes.

The right hon. gentleman has suggested that the only piece of legislation the opposition held up was redistribution. Does the right hon. gentleman think that a minority in the house, if it disagrees with something, has the right indefinitely to refuse the majority the right to express its views through a vote?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman will receive his answer in a few moments, when I deal with the words of a parliamentarian with whom I am sure the hon. member will agree, irrespective of his feelings. I refer to Right Hon. Mackenzie King. I will deal with that subject when I reach it.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I did not make the question clear to the right hon. gentleman. I should make it clear that

I was referring in my question to the redistribution matter.

Yes. Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has a way about him, and I do not take him any more seriously than he sometimes is taken outside the house. I did say to him courteously that I would deal with his question, but then he ran away from it by asking another question.
Mr. Speaker, he brings me to this position. In spite of all the Liberal mythology in relation to parliament being brought to an impasse, who brought it here? Did we bring in the Prime Minister's personal choice? Did we prevent him bringing in legislation regarding the economy, the necessity of expansion of trade, and the subject of the question raised by the hon. member for Perth, in reference to the declaration of national goals? Who brought about division within this country? Who created it or, if not created, who added the fires to division? We have never seen anything to equal the separation, the division, the antagonisms expressed within our country that we have seen since the present government came into office. One of the major reasons is this: They promised everything and they have executed little or nothing.
It was not the Conservative party that had the separatists. It was not the Conservative party that had an hon. member in their midst who would abolish the Queen and remove the British connection. I thought that hon. member was speaking for himself, but in the last 10 days it is apparent that he has become a paragon of perfection as he moves around, interrupts and receives the warmest plaudits from those who I would have thought would have contemptuously spumed one who expressed views such as he is expressing.
Did we bring about the bitter division? Sir, this parliament has a great responsibility. Some newspaper editorials say: Mind you, the Prime Minister made a mistake, he should not have got us into this, but the opposition is terrible because it dares to stand against his personal desires. Sir, we have no excuses to offer. An hon. gentleman says, should it not be brought to a vote? Shades of Laurier and Borden. I have two volumes here that I am sure will take their place alongside the volume on Mr. King that was edited by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill).
I make an appeal to the government. I know it is late to do it but we have a sacred trust. Do not let us continue this course and

build up controversies for the future. We believe that policy should bring Canadians together rather than disintegrate them. All of this was encouraged by the Prime Minister when he made that speech in the month of April after the election, in which he said he believed in two nations. That is when the trouble began. In other parts of Canada it was explained that he really had not meant it. In the House of Commons one Friday he came forward with a commission to investigate separatism but when he saw the effect of it somebody issued a press release that night.
Who has been building up false hopes for the people? What about the wild and unrestrained statements that have been made by influential men not in the Conservative party? It is not being anti-Quebec to say that certain men have spoken in a way that cannot help but divide this country. Yet when one takes that stand it is argued that one is anti-Quebec. Not at all; I have never in my life uttered a word that could be so construed.
I go back to 1924 when I took a case in the province of Saskatchewan on behalf of French school trustees. I was told: Do not take it; it will cause you difficulty in the future. Sir, I have never failed to take the stand which I believed was necessary and proper. When I spoke, as did many members of the N.D.P., regarding the injustice done to the Japanese Canadians, their only offence their colour, I was alone among my colleagues. When in June of 1940 I made a speech for the first time in the House of Commons I appealed then for a Canadianism. At that time terrible criticisms were being uttered against those of German origin. I said: These people are Canadians. It was not popular to take that stand.
I recollect what happened in 1961 and 1962 when I said that we must have a colourblind commonwealth. What did hon. gentlemen opposite say? They said that I lost favour with the United Kingdom; but today this is accepted. Speaking for this party and the government of that day, I said to the British people in 1962: You have full right as an independent country to join the common market but you have responsibilities to the commonwealth which you yourselves have admitted and we ask you not to forget the institution that above everything else in the world represents something that no other group of nations has ever been able to achieve. I was criticized; I was bitterly denounced. Do you hear any of those opposite saying today that they want to get into the
Canadian Flag
common market? Today they are using the arguments for which they criticized us. Great is the experience of public life when you see people sitting opposite who in the month of May, 1962, said that nothing more terrible had ever happened than the pegging of the Canadian dollar but who now embrace the heresy of those days as their own.
One must take a stand. One cannot always be on the side of a majority, but when there is a great principle at stake parties have a responsibility. A very prominent Conservative wrote me and said: Don't fight them, they are thirsty for this flag; let them have it and when a change of government comes bring in your own flag. The hon. gentleman says, let us get to a vote, because he has the artificial certainty of a quiescent majority with him. Sir, that is not parliament, as I will show when I refer to the words of Laurier.
I want to see this institution not derided, not downgraded. There are one or two who are doing so whose knowledge of democracy is not in keeping with their enthusiasm for condemnation of the Conservative party. The relation of parliament to public opinion is a serious matter. That is why the press has its place. The elector requires and is entitled to a fair and impartial view of what is going on in parliament. I ask you, sir. Is it a fair division when the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, on the day when two speeches were made, one by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) and the other by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) speaking from the wells of experience, those wells from which his people have drawn their sustenance and power for a thousand years, should devote to one speech eight times the amount of attention devoted to the other?
Typical.

That is one-sided. No one can argue that it is not. And you will never build a Canada if information is to be denied when it is critical of a government, but given first place when it consists of the declarations of a government. I speak realizing that what I say may be misinterpreted. But I do not want to be misinterpreted. I want to say this finally and unequivocally-that only now, in the last week or so, is the feeling getting through to the people.
I should like to read what some of the hon. gentlemen opposite are hearing from their constituents. "Get to a vote". Yes. If they would heed the call of their constituents it will be of interest when they do vote. We

Canadian Flag
must work tor national unity. We did. When were in office, we tried to unify. We made the House of Commons a living place when we installed the simultaneous translation system. Today there is a degree of exchange which never took place before in this house. We did not contribute to separating the people of our country on the basis of race, religion, or province against province. Somebody will argue: Oh, if you only fall in line with this and allow the three maple leaves, all will be well. Mr. Speaker, the niggling knife would still continue. I said I would be restrained in what I have to say in the absence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) because I will be able to say more when he is back. But I find it difficult to explain why, knowing in advance that there was going to be division, he got into this and carried his supporters along, the speed of the caravan being determined by the right hon. gentleman.
I do not intend to follow on this occasion the sinuous course the government has followed. The Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) is not here; I will have some reference to make to him when he is. But I simply point out in this regard the fact that what has happened is now being blamed on us, because we dared to stand. Well, last evening I read the words of Ulysses, which are the embodiment of our attitude-"strong in will to strive, to seek, to find and not to yield". Members opposite thought they would dominate us by a campaign of vituperation the like of which I have not seen in this land. I do not complain, but I point out that this is the situation. Sir, why did they do it? Why did they act? Why did not the Prime Minister, unless he wanted to make a political matter of this, go to the leaders of the various parties before the seeds of dissension had been planted by his aggressive speech in Winnipeg to the Royal Canadian Legion? Can we not sit down together and talk things over? Was there any attitude of compromise when, knowing that he had a multitude with him, he could ride roughshod? We said, no.
Sir, have we a national flag, a distinctive flag? I ask you to turn to the answer given by Mr. St. Laurent as prime minister in 1951, on November 21 when he was asked the question:
What steps are being taken by the government with respect to the adoption of a distinctive national flag?
To that question, his answer was: "See order in council P.C. 5888 of September 15, 1945."

Why did they do this? What did they think they would achieve? Why do they now try to blame us for standing in the way of one of the most barefaced attempts in Canadian history to overwhelm an opposition which represents millions of Canadians? Again, I ask the question: Why? You do not choose a flag that way. You do not change a flag in the systole and diastole of political controversy following an election. This is something for Canada's next hundred years. Yet the government decided for political purposes -that is what La Presse said-for the prospect of votes, to bring about a stifling of the outpouring of the spirit of millions of Canadians. And they did it by fooling the people of the province of Quebec. I have had a great deal of correspondence from that province lately and the question asked me is this-
What is the constituency of my hon. friend-
Oh, oh.

Yes, that is one of my
afflictions; I can never remember the names of constituencies. I have not that kind of memory, though hon. members opposite may have it. But I remember the great things, and the great principles, and this is something they might bear in mind.
Hear, hear.

Can you imagine hon. gentlemen opposite-I would like to identify them if they would let me know who they are, so that they would be on the record- when we are discussing a matter of importance to Canadians as a whole indulging in that kind of exhibitionism?
Shame.

There is no identification. Their silence is their own rebuke. What they are trying to do is to cover up their failure to act on so many matters that desperately need to be solved, and they bring up an issue of an emotional nature to conceal their failure.
I do not want to impose anything on the people of Quebec. I have acted for the French Canadians through the years. As one gets on to my time in life he can look back. I have acted for them throughout the years. I know them. I do not want to impose. That is not the spirit of 100 years ago today-to impose. Neither do I want them to say to the rest of Canada. "We must do this." I am sure they do not have that view. This is not a country that can be governed by the imposition of brute force.

Sir, I speak with more emotion than usual when I think of what is being done to this, my country. I am of mixed origin too. I am not one with a colonial viewpoint. Conservative prime ministers and leaders from Macdonald to date have not been colonialists. They have led the way on behalf of an independent nation.
Hear, hear.
Hear, hear.

Sir, when I say that, I also want to add that we are prepared at all times as Canadians to hold out the right hand of fellowship in a spirit of compromise, for after all this is a country where compromise is of the essence, so long as compromise does not violate principles.
I have not forgotten the question put by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill). I shall come to that rather too soon for him.
You cannot come to it too soon.

He was one of the devotees, one who was described by pamphleteers as the power behind Mr. King. I see he wags his head in a horizontal position. Such modesty is unusual even though unvoiced. Sir, on August 11, 1944, near the end of the war, I spoke immediately before the prime minister, who was my member. We had that relationship of member and constituent that did not

always bear the relationship of Damon and Pythias, but Mr. King had his views. Let me read what he said. In my remarks, I mentioned that, when our men came back from overseas, let them be Canadian. I am not going to quote my speech. I have never made a habit of doing that, but I preceded him, contending that we should build Canada with Canadians, maintaining the constitutional rights by assuring to those of us in whose veins flowed blood not entirely British or French equal rights as citizens, equal rights as Canadians, and Mr. King said:
May I say to my hon. friend that in that I am in entire and wholehearted agreement with him.
I cannot express too strongly the feeling I have that some of these practices which have been carried on by the census branch for statistical purposes, or possibly for ethnological purposes-
I believe that is the way it is described-might be done away with. I would be happy to join with my hon. friend and with any others in seeking to do my part to see absolute recognition, or recognition made in an absolute way of men and women who were bom in this country, and those who have become Canadian citizens being regarded as Canadians first, foremost and all the time.
Sir, what do the three maple leaves typify? The Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) in his speech to the philatelic organization, said one stands for the British, one stands for the French and the other stands for the other racial origins. He never got to telling them what the centre one stood for. It was nonsense.
Were they thinking about other ethnic groups in Quebec in 1868 when they came out with their coat of arms? Were they thinking of them in Ontario? Not at all.
As a matter of fact this flag was first placed on a stamp as a result of the action of the Postmaster General after he took office. He told us the other day it had been decided in July of 1963. That is what he told the house, but he forgot what he said in the month of April. I will read what he said then, according to Southam news services:
Postmaster General John R. Nicholson, however, said he knew nothing about this design representing the new Canadian flag, although he chose the stamp and decided its colours himself after entering office last February 1.
Ten days ago he told us he had nothing to do with it, that it had been decided before any question of a change of flag was being considered. Then listen to these words:
Mr. Nicholson admitted that it had been proposed that the stamp be issued with the maple leaves red on a white background, but he decided to try a little background colour.

"I thought of that pale blue they use in the United Nations flag," he said-
I say to him, on the basis of his statement of April 17, that this was just part of the propaganda to soften up the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
Good.
The right hon. gentleman is glibly suggesting that the statement I made here in all sincerity is not true, that it is hypocritical.
I did not say either of those things.

I did say the maple leaf design was chosen in or about the month of July, 1963. The records of the Post Office Department show that. I did make a modest contribution to the final design when I learned, through technical advice, that there was a question of whether a red stamp on a white background could be picked up electronically. After I became Postmaster General I directed that a colour change be made from a white background to a blue background. That is the simple explanation.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, it is a simple explanation but it is far removed from the explanation of April 17 that appeared in the Canadian Press. But I am really not concerned about that, because all the minister has succeeded in doing is assure the house that he was not one of the four wise men who induced the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to accept the three maple leaf design.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the right hon. gentleman would permit me to ask him a question?
No. If the hon. gentleman would-
I am asking if the right hon. gentleman will permit me-
Sit down.
He isn't speaking to the subamendment.
Order. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition is making a speech.
Hear, hear.
Oh, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) said I am not on the subamendment. I am glad he raised that point.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I know the right hon. gentleman suffers from the same defect I do, that of hardness of hearing; but that does not excuse his misrepresenting what I said. I asked the right hon. gentleman, very politely, if I could ask him a question and I made no other remark of any kind. And I was denied the question.

I hasten immediately, Mr. Speaker, to say that if the hon. gentleman says he did not make that remark, I accept it; but it just shows the influence he has on backbench members, one of whom has a voice that sounds very much like his, apparently in emulation. I was reading what Mr. King said, and I would have thought it would have commanded the attention of the Minister of Transport. Mr. King said:
And may I say this to my hon. friend, that he has touched upon a very real subject, when he speaks of men who have fought and died as Canadians, irrespective of race and religion. X regret much to see in this country at the present time some gentlemen who are in positions of high respect, and who know better, seeking to raise matters of creed and race, with the suggestion that things are being done for people of one area rather than for those of another. May I say to this committee that if anyone wishes a battle on the question of whether we are to have one part of this country singled out as non-Canadian as against what by others is said to be Canadian, no one would welcome that fight any more than I would.
And anyone who raises the question of race to prejudice anyone of another race in this country is doing the greatest disservice that can be done to Canadian unity and to Canadian nationality. And not only do I wish to see our people recognized as Canadians, but I also wish to see a Canadian flag recognized in this country. I would like to see it the flag that our Canadian men are fighting under today. We have a Canadian flag unfurled in battle today by our very brave men in Italy and in France. I think in time the people of this country of Canada will say we want to have as a Canadian flag the flag they are carrying in battle today.
Hear, hear.

That is No. 1. Then they say we have not a distinctive flag. That is not what Mr. King said. And what did Mr. St. Laurent say? I want to nail down these misconceptions and falsifications that are being bandied about. Mr. St. Laurent said on November 13, 1945, with regard to a distinctive flag and a design for it, that any such design should include the union jack in the upper left corner. That was Mr. St. Laurent. Was he any less a Canadian for saying that? Then he went on to say that the question of a flag "should be lifted above the plane of partisan politics." Sir,

how much I agree with that view. This design was put forward by the Prime Minister for political purposes and now, finding himself in difficulties, who is blamed? We are blamed for not letting him do that. What a hypocritical stand to take. Let me read further what Mr. St. Laurent said. They say that to have the union jack on the flag is a mark of subservience and domination. What did Mr. St. Laurent say, as is reported at page 2096 of Hansard:
I do not think any member of this honourable house would quarrel with that statement.
He is referring to the preceding statement, whatever it was:
The union jack is a symbol which represents much that is best in the heritage of all those who derive their traditions and their culture from western Europe.
Then he said:
I do not believe that any of us in this country at this time regard the union jack as being a symbol of conquest or a symbol of subjugation. It is under the union jack that the institutions of this Canadian nation have grown and developed and have brought us to the point where now, and for a good many years now, the dominion is and has been an autonomous state subject in no phase of its domestic or of its external affairs to any other authority-
Then he quoted with approval Mr. King's words to the Canadian Legion.
Mr. King assured the Legion officers that, so far as he was concerned, the new Canadian flag should certainly contain the union jack. It might be debatable whether a single maple leaf in the fly would be preferable to the Canadian coat of arms at present incorporated in the Canadian red ensign, but it would be unthinkable to have a flag for this dominion that did not contain the union jack.
Hear, hear.

That was Mr. King's stand, and certainly throughout his life he stood for independence, and strongly stood for it. In this regard Mr. St. Laurent said:
I am prepared to say now that I for one fully share the views expressed by the prime minister to this delegation, the legionnaires-
There are those who tell you, sir, and try to lead Canadians to believe that we are pushing something on Quebec. Who was in the cabinet then? Mr. King was the prime minister, there was Mr. St. Laurent, and Mr. Lesage was in the cabinet. Did we have anything to do with this flag that was recommended, with the fact that the red ensign should be the flag-

Mr. Speaker, this is one time that the hon. gentleman's memory regarding this question is correct. But Mr. Lesage was in the house. Did he raise any objection?
He was honestly silent.

He was never one not to
speak what he thought. I have placed these quotations before the house, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose of answering this kind of propaganda that the Liberal party has disseminated, namely that we are trying to push something on Quebec. It was done when the hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. The Minister of Transport was the grey eminence-although not grey-behind Mr. Mackenzie King.
I was asked by the hon. gentleman what the attitude would be as to an opposition that stands for the things that it believes in, in principle. I do not refer to questions of ordinary, every day economics but to matters that affect a nation, its well-being, its future -everything that we hold dear. I would ask him to read the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, because they represent a viewpoint that cannot be gainsaid. He pointed out during the course of his statement in this House of Commons when the house was discussing the navy bill, debate on which lasted for months and months in 1912-13, that an opposition has the right to act when there is a question of principle at stake. In the course of his remarks he dealt particularly with what had happened in the past. In 1912 the Conservative party under Sir Robert Borden brought in legislation to provide for naval assistance to the United Kingdom. Sir Wilfrid has always been regarded by friend and foe as a great parliamentarian. I read from the "Life and letters of Sir Wilfrid Laurier", volume 2. I have Hansard in my office, but not having brought it down with me I will read from this volume. At page 409 the following appears:
Amendment after amendment was made, only to be voted down.
That was by the Liberal party of the day.
Every naval commander from Noah to Nelson was quoted and quoted again. Conservatives ceased to speak and Liberals spoke double time. Tempers rose, interruption was frequent, the Speaker "named" members, and still little progress was made with the bill. Finally, the government decided to force the bill through under closure.
That is when Sir Wilfrid gave not only Canada of his day but posterity the answer to those who talk of filibuster. They did not use that expression then. Filibuster is an

Canadian Flag
had its place. The present government, alter an election, decided to give their own definition to "distinctive", and their definition is one without any recognition of the heritage of the past, the devotion of either French or English to our country.
There are others who insist on the red ensign without change or modification. There are some who in the interests of unity, and I plead that, are prepared to agree to modifications that will recognize the contributions of the two great races. There are some who want the three maple leaf flag. There are others who want a one maple leaf flag. Then, sir, there are some in all these categories who have been shocked at the course that the Liberal party took in bringing this flag before us.
The Canadian people have a right to say what kind of flag they want and they can only exercise that right through a plebiscite. But in the interests of bringing us together I repeat the suggestion of a committee, but not one to meet for three or four weeks. Her Majesty will be here on the 12th of October and such a committee does not have to be limited to that date. Let it sit for three months. Certainly I think it would take two months. The question of time is not important, but the committee should not be directed that it has to do the job within a certain time. If the committee comes up with a substantial majority, then there is no need for further argument. A short debate would be sufficient. But, sir, unless it does we are back to where we were, except that we have given Canadians a chance to think this over.
Feeling has crystallized very strongly in the last few weeks. So far as time is concerned, I have read one commentator, who in the past has achieved monetary gain by libellous statements, who says that it is costing $33,000 a day for parliament to sit. That is absolutely false. Our salaries are spread over the year. It does not cost any more for parliament to sit today than if we were home, except for the paper, the printing, the page boys and the like. That statement is a complete fabrication. If we were home all of the staff here with few exceptions, as you know, Mr. Speaker, would still be on salary. That statement is designed to hurt and to damage, and the truth can never catch up to a falsehood. But that statement should be answered. In addition, sir, I do not think that anybody should object to sitting, with the salary that is being received today, and I speak as one who does not receive the addition. Parliament is not to be measured by cost. Parliament

is to be measured by the degree to which it brings about improvement for the benefit of the nation.
We are ready. Bring on your legislative program. We will be glad to pass it as we have passed other measures. The government have nothing ready except that in their minds they have got plans. If they have anything ready, let them bring it forward. What is there to stop them bringing in the resolution on pensions which has so frequently been asked for? Let us deal with that. Let us set up the committee and let the committee go to work. The government has endeavoured to lead the Canadian people to believe that we are preventing them from bringing in anything. We will welcome legislation. Bring it in and we will give a legislative program every support. But I want to brand as another myth the suggestion that while we debate this matter that will affect Canadians for 100 years we are holding up other legislation.
Sir, you cannot make a flag for a country by putting a slug of political advantage into a jukebox. That is what they are trying to do. The Prime Minister looked over this flag and he said, "I hanker for it". What would this committee do? Would it not consider the indicia of a flag? In the darkest days of 1915 when the British and French had their backs to the wall President Woodrow Wilson spoke of the flag as the embodiment not of sentiment but of history.
I do not want to say anything critical about the three maple leaves, but does it move your heart to see this flag after it has flown for a week or ten days? Does it touch you as freedom's banner streaming o'er us? Does it consecrate in everyone looking at it the history, the struggle, the strife that brought about our Canada? Sir, a flag cannot be created by one man however powerful his position. This is a time of instant creation but you cannot create instant flags. Flags are born in the strife and turmoil of clash of history. They are not the result of an egocentric decision.
That is why we have taken this stand, Mr. Speaker. I speak again as one of two racial origins, neither one of which ever could be dominated. My paternal ancestors came here 150 years ago and until I became prime minister it was often said it could never be that one of German or Dutch origin could be prime minister. My highland ancestors were not dominated. The English tried to dominate them after Culloden. They directed that they could not wear the kilt or sound the pibroch, and the Bannermans were at Culloden. The

penalty was death. It did not mean anything. They stood because those things represented something to them, the richness of their past. They arouse the sacred emotion of loyalty. I plead with the government: Do not push on with this.
Today the Prime Minister meets with the premiers of the provinces. I will be the first to congratulate him if they bring about today something that we tried for and did not succeed in accomplishing. That is the history of mankind. Some try, and we advance. They have not lost because they do not attain. This is a step forward. If we get this accomplished, then let us together, in a spirit of Canadianism, a spirit of give and take, bring about a flag which will not disunite, as will this creation that is before us, but which will within its folds gather us all together so that in the next hundred years this country's destiny will be that for which we all hope.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Acting Prime Minister):
speechtext:
When the right hon. gentleman began to speak I had no thought of taking any part in the debate on this subamendment which, it seems to me, we could best debate by deciding, because it concerns a purely technical problem. It is not the real issue before us. The real issue lies in the resolution itself, not in the subamendment or even in the amendment.
But the right hon. gentleman made one statement which, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is not here, I feel should be corrected. He said that at no time before the elections of 1962 or 1963 did the Prime Minister make it clear in public what he meant by a distinctive flag. I know that the right hon. gentleman did not knowingly-
I will immediately withdraw if the hon. gentleman can show me I was wrong. I have every one of the quotations.

The right hon. gentleman might have every one of the quotations, in which case he must have mislaid the two I am about to put on record now. I think every hon. member will consider it desirable that they be put on record so that there will be no further inadvertent misquotation or misrepresentation.
On January 21, 1960, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, speaking on the program called "The Nation's Business" said- and I wish to quote one sentence from his remarks at that time:
We must agree on a distinctive national flag which cannot be mistaken lor an emblem of
Canadian Flag
any other country and which is accepted as such by the Canadian people.
Now, the Prime Minister was asked by a number of people to interpret precisely what he meant by the phrase "a distinctive national flag which cannot be mistaken for an emblem of any other country". And on January 27, from the office of the leader of the opposition he issued a statement which I intend to read.
What year was that?

This was in 1960. So that there may be no doubt whatever about where my right hon. friend stood, here is the statement:
In the reference which I made in my television talk on "The Nation's Business" series on January 21 to a national flag for Canada. I was concerned with the desirability of the Canadian government taking full responsibility as soon as possible for finding a solution to the flag problem by submitting to parliament a measure which-if accepted by the representatives of the people in parliament- would, I hope, settle the problem.
The present red ensign has never been given formal sanction by parliament. Furthermore (I know this from my own correspondence) it is not approved by a great many Canadians as a national flag because, in design, it is the same as the United Kingdom merchant marine flag, with the Canadian coat of arms added. The two flags can be mistaken for each other, and there are many who think that this confusion should be removed. There is no such confusion in any other part of the commonwealth, because each country, including Australia and New Zealand, has a flag which is easily identifiable with its country and cannot be mistaken for that of any other country.
The union jack, a flag which every Canadian should honour and respect, is not however acceptable to many Canadians as a distinctive national flag of Canada because it is also the distinctive national flag of the United Kingdom. In consequence as I have indicated above, there is an unfortunate division of opinion in this country on the flag question. The time has come, I think, when this situation should be cleared up by governmental initiative and parliamentary action.
Indeed, whatever action parliament might take in regard to a Canadian flag, I believe that the union jack should be accepted by Canada as an emblem to be flown on all occasions which are concerned with our commonwealth association and our status as a monarchy with the Queen as the head of that commonwealth.
When the present Prime Minister said this in 1960, it was accepted, and that position was accepted by the Liberal party, and it was the position we took at the election of 1962. It was in our literature.
Not at all.
In exactly the same words, that was in our literature in 1963.

No.
