No one can say I did not
listen intently, or with courtesy and politeness, to the right hon. gentleman when he was speaking, as did my hon. triends, and I think I might be permitted to say what I have to say without these noisy interruptions. What I say seems not to be palatable, but it happens to be the simple truth. I will bring these statements down at eight o'clock and if anyone wishes me to do so, I will table them. Each of these statements has been circulated throughout the country. One of them has been handed to me, now-
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

Not at the moment. I think the hon. member has not been recognized by the Chair.
This is from the 1963 program under the heading "Adopt a Distinctive Canadian Flag and Anthem".
Within two years of taking office, a new Liberal government will submit to parliament a design for a ffag which cannot be mistaken for the emblem of any other country. When adopted this will be the flag of Canada. "O Canada" will be proclaimed our official anthem.
The union jack will be flown on appropriate occasions as a symbol of our membership in the commonwealth. A new Liberal government will also maintain the honour given to the traditional anthem which expresses Canada's devotion to the sovereign.
This document was published. It is published all over this country and nobody on earth has any right to say that we did not make our position clear in two general elections.
Hear, hear.
We did that, sir, and I suggest we had a perfect right to place that program before parliament.
Order please. There is a point of order by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.

I rise on a point of order because of the reference made to myself by the Minister of Transport when he told the house that I had not been given recognition by the Chair. I recall, sir, that within the last two days the Chair gave a specific-
Sit down.

Order please. There is no point of order there. I am sure the hon. member does not wish to interrupt the Acting Prime Minister. No one interrupted the

right hon. Leader of the Opposition and I think we should have a little fair play.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I wish to mention in my point of order that there was a ruling given by the Chair within the last two days which indicated that a member rising on a question had the right to the floor provided the hon. member speaking would yield the floor to him. That was the ruling by the Chair with respect to a question put the other day. The Chair ruled that a member had the right to ask a question if the hon. member speaking yielded. I would also remind the Minister of Transport that on two occasions he was permitted to interrupt the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. The floor was yielded to him.
In this particular case the floor was not yielded by the hon. member who was speaking.

Mr. Speaker, I am rather astonished that after all the appeals from the other side for someone on this side to speak, when someone on this side tries to speak he is not permitted to continue.
It would be rather redundant, but I could go on and put on the record precisely the same words that were in the program of 1962. I think that disposes pretty conclusively of this talk about the resolution which stands in my right hon. friend's name being anything personal.
This resolution was not merely put on the order paper with the full authority of the government, by the head of the government, but it was put on with the full authority of the Liberal party, passed through all those channels used to put a program before the people of this country in two elections in which we were participating. And in order to make it clear it was neither personal, nor even for that matter governmental, at the request of hon. gentlemen opposite, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has indicated there will be a completely free vote on this matter and that the government would not consider its life at stake.
If hon. gentlemen opposite are so afraid that hon. members in other parts of the house- I do not mean just on this side-will express opinions different from theirs, if they are allowed free expression of opinion, then that is an odd conception of that democracy of which the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said he had so much knowledge. It seems to me, sir, that the proper conception of democracy is that under a system of delegated

democracy, which any parliamentary system is, programs are put before the people. A government is chosen, and if that government puts matters before parliament it should have a right at least to have the voice of parliament on those matters after there has been all the debate there can reasonably be.
I am not one of those who think there should be any restriction on the right of any member in this house to express his own opinions on the flag. But I may say I think it rather astonishing that all these letters from other people, and newspaper comments which we can all read anyway and which, under our rules of debate we are not supposed to inject into debate, seem to be a large part of many of the speeches made. Indeed I am rather surprised that they are represented as a contribution, a personal contribution coming from the heart, particularly in cases when a sheet of paper is lost and the heart stops beating until it can be recovered from the floor.
Hear, hear.

I endorse the words of the right hon. gentleman opposite when he said we want consent in this house, not domination. I agree. We do not want to be dominated by a man who is dominating a minority in this house and preventing the majority from expressing its views. I am not going to take up the time of the house by quoting gossip columnists about anonymous members in the Tory backbenches and what they think about their leader. Picking up gossip and retailing it about anonymous people strikes me as being a rather second rate form of debate, and that is what the right hon. gentleman opposite did.
He also said that one man was not going to be allowed to impose his flag on this country. Sir, I hope that the people of Canada are not going to allow one man, drunk for power, to prevent the people of this country from having a flag if they want one.
The right hon. gentleman has found in my old master, Mr. Mackenzie King, a patron saint for the Tory party. I may say this is not untypical of Tories; to wear the worn out clothes of Liberals to cover their nakedness. I remember the enthusiasm with which the Tory party greeted Mr. Mackenzie King's initiative in 1945. They called it separatism and accused him of breaking up the empire. They said this red ensign was the end of all we held dear, that we must stick by the union jack. Now Mr. Mackenzie King is their hero.
The right hon. gentleman, Mr. Speaker, saw fit to degrade those three maple leaves which have been the emblem of this country since

confederation and which the right hon. gentleman, himself, when he was prime minister had cast in bronze-they can be seen in room 16-as a symbol of Canada.
The right hon. gentleman, when he was prime minister, proudly had them put on his motor car-before the days of stickers.
Hear, hear.
He approved the Queen putting them on the royal standard. He put them on a postage stamp long before my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) was postmaster general.
When?
The hon. gentleman can do his own research on that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Give us the facts.

All right. It was in 1959, when the right hon. gentleman was prime minister, that the three maple leaves conjoined on a single stem were put on a postage stamp of Canada, and the word "Canada" proudly underneath, and the prime minister of that time is now the Leader of the Opposition.
Hear, hear.

That is the plain fact. Sir, one thing that does shock me, and I think it shocks a great many other Canadians who have memories, too, that this maple leaf symbol of ours which is associated with Vimy ridge, which is associated with Dieppe, which is associated with every glorious feat of arms of this country-and in our short history we have had many of them-that hon. gentlemen have sought in this debate to degrade it. I think that is shameful; I hope it will not continue. Let us by all means differ, but let us try to avoid in this debate, on both sides of the house, casting any aspersions on the cherished views of others.
For myself, I do not have a very mixed origin. I am mostly a rather stolid, rather stupid Anglo-Saxon, but I also have a little Dutch blood and I am not ashamed of it. I do not think it has ever prevented me from doing anything I have wanted to do. But I do say, sir, that for me the union jack is the symbol of the land of my ancestors, and I think that land is as good a country as any other in the world, except Canada. But it is not the symbol of Canada-and the maple leaf is.

Hear, hear.

Canadian Flag

I can tell the right hon. gentleman, if he does not know it already, why there is unity in the Liberal party and among its members in this house with regard to this question. There is not unity in his party, and if he doubts it, let him ask the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bal-cer). I will tell the whole house why there is unity in the Liberal party on this question. It is because we did what has been done time and again in the history of this country. It was done at Charlottetown, Quebec and at the Westminster Palace hotel and was embodied in the British North America Act. We agreed on a compromise. That was set out in the program that we honestly and straightforwardly put forward to the Canadian people in two elections. We said we wanted a Canadian flag that was Canadian, and we wanted to fly the union jack, or a flag containing the uion jack, to symbolize our association with the commonwealth and our monarchical character and devotion to the crown. I say, Mr. Speaker, that is a position that is honourable, that is loyal and that, above all, is Canadian.
I certainly would not wish anything I might say to appear to deny to any hon. member in any part of the house his full right to express his views and to express them fully on this question. But we are not debating the flag question at the moment; we are debating a subamendment, a technical subamendment, to an amendment. This subamendment concerns a plebiscite. The right hon. gentleman talked about where his party stood. Well, where do they stand? They have never told us what kind of flag they want, because they cannot agree, because they will not agree, because the section of the party led by the hon. member for Three Rivers cannot agree with what the right hon. gentleman wants. This is not a secret. I suggest that the main reason hon. gentlemen opposite are not willing to allow the rest of us to express our opinions by a vote is because a vote would reveal the hopeless division in their own party.
Hear, hear.

But I suggest to the right hon. gentleman that we go ahead and have a vote on this subamendment and the amendment, on which there is no question of principle involved at all, and then we go on to deal with the main motion. There has only been one speaker on the main motion so far, and that is the right hon. gentleman himself. I suggest that we debate the main motion and when there has been the fullest possible de-

bate, that, like adults, we decide this question; like the other great questions that other parliaments in this country in other times have been called upon to decide. I suggest, sir, that this is the way to make parliament work and to make parliament respected.
I agree with the right hon. gentleman when he said this was an important question. I have no patience with those who say it is an unimportant question and we should get on with other matters that are more important. There is no more important question than any question which affects the basic unity of our country. We will not have much of a Canada pension plan if we have not a united country to support it; we will not have much of a railway policy. I might say, en passant, that if the right hon. gentleman will carry out his word when I bring this important railway legislation forward-and it has been ready for months-and put it through, I will be most grateful to him.
Bring it in.
If he will do the same with regard to redistribution-a principle that he claims the parentage of, but he does not want his child to be born-if he will let it be born, we will appreciate it.
Bring it forward.
Well, settle this question. This is the basic question.
Hear, hear.

I suggest that those hon. gentlemen opposite who can read should read the order paper. They will see what is on it already. There is plenty to do. But, Mr. Speaker, having undertaken this task, surely we can find it possible to act like adults in this house and settle this matter in an adult fashion. I suggest that no minority and, above all, no minority dominated-apparently all but bewitched, by one man-

-should consider that it has a right to prevent the equal right of everyone in this house to express himself in the only way in which we can all express ourselves, and that is by a vote. That, after all, is perhaps the characteristic of our civilization. In four fifths of the world the people cannot do what we can do here in this house; they cannot settle their own destiny and they cannot get rid of the people who do it badly, either. In four fifths of the world the only way to get rid of a government you do not like is by violence and force.

The whole basis of our system is, as the right hon. gentleman said, consent and not domination.
However, Mr. Speaker, this kind of system will only work when we all honestly and loyally resolve to make it work. There is no system easier than the parliamentary system to disrupt, if the desire to disrupt is there. I appeal to hon. gentlemen: make all your speeches; say everything that is in your hearts; do your best to get your way-but if you cannot get your way, accept the democratic way and allow these matters to be settled, like adults.
By bringing in closure again?

Mr. Speaker, I think an hon. gentleman said something about closure. I have said nothing about closure. I do not think any of us should even be thinking about closure; I think what we should be thinking about is resolving this question. Certainly, sir, there is no reason whatsoever why we should not dispose of the subamendment and the amendment and then, if someone else has another amendment to move, deal with that. I dare say there will be several amendments. There is going to be a free vote; my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has said that. If hon. gentlemen opposite have any united conviction about a flag, there is nothing to stop them moving an amendment to the Prime Minister's motion and putting it to the test of this house.
I hope we will have, after today, an end to these reflections upon the motives of our fellow members of parliament. Mr. Speaker, I have sought in what I have said to reflect in no way upon the motives of hon. gentlemen opposite, except possibly in the case of the right hon. gentleman, the early part of whose speech was a reflection upon everybody on this side of the house, and a deliberate reflection upon them. I have not done that and I do not intend to. But I do suggest that we rise above that kind of thing. Even though we feel strongly and differ on this question we are all honest in our differences, and I suggest that we settle this thing like Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) a question. I am sure we are all grateful to him for setting out the ideas the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) had when he was leader of the opposition in respect to the flag situation and the national anthem. It was set out very clearly that the union jack would

denote our commonwealth association and that "O Canada" would be our national anthem. Then he mentioned a distinctive Canadian flag. I wonder whether perchance he missed the paragraph where the flag was described as a three maple leaves flag.

No, Mr. Speaker. I am speaking from memory, but I do not think my memory is too bad, and I have always had a disposition in this house to correct a mistake if I make one. I am sure all hon. members will agree with that. However, my memory is that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister said on a good many occasions that he felt the only way this question could be resolved was to have a design put before parliament for parliament to decide. There is the greatest liberty being given to this House of Commons. We have a design put forward by my right hon. friend as head of the government. He has now said that the government will not consider its life at stake in this matter. Therefore it is open to any hon. member who wishes to do so-as the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) has publicly indicated he wishes to-to propose a substitution for that flag. Now, what could be freer than that?
Would the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) permit a question now?
Yes.

The minister indicated to the house that during the last two elections the Liberal party advocated both in their literature and otherwise a distinctive Canadian flag. He said that this is the simple truth. Is the minister now saying that the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) was lying to the house on August 24?

Mr. Speaker, I really do not think I need make any comments on the speech of the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), because if I did I might be tempted to say something about the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) and I do not want to create that kind of atmosphere in the house this afternoon.
A supplementary question. Is the minister aware that what he has said this afternoon is in direct contradiction of what the hon. member for York-Humber said on August 24?
No. I have not read the speech of the hon. member for York-Humber.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask a question of the Minister of Transport. I should like to verify whether what I thought I heard is correct. The minister read two statements made by the leader of his party, and in the second one it seemed to me that he designated the flags of New Zealand and Australia as the type of distinctive national flag which cannot be mistaken for the flag of any other country. If that is the case, would the minister not agree that this gives no indication that the union jack would be removed from such a flag? The hon. member will be able to read in Hansard what was said and can draw his own inferences from that; but I do not draw that inference from it and I do not think anyone else did. I remember very well the statement; and when you remember the fact that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister also said we should fly the union jack, that seems to be a clear indication that the union jack would not be in the national flag.
Oh, oh.
Well, I do not think that any person who wanted to accept those words in the sense in which they were written would have had any doubt whatever about them.
Then why didn't he spell it out?

The hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) asked the question from his seat: Why did the right hon. gentleman not spell it out? He did spell it out. Why does not the right hon. gentleman opposite spell out the flag that his party stands for? I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker: It is because they do not stand for one at all.
Our flag is the people's choice.
Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, I
am the last one who would enter this debate with any idea of prolonging it unnecessarily, as all hon. members know. I have a suggestion which I am going to make to the house which might be an acceptable compromise to resolve this rather acrimonious debate which has now gone on for the best part of three weeks. I should like to say that this is the first time that I have participated in the debate on the flag.
Before making the suggestion which I propose to make for the consideration of the house I think that some of the accusations and statements made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) who has just resumed his seat should not be allowed to pass unchallenged. He has, for instance, stated that many members have spoken in breach of the rules of this house by reading from letters received from their constituents, from newspaper reports and the like. Yet the minister himself has just finished reading from a Liberal document supplied to him by one of

his backbenchers. I believe the rules stipulate that it is proper for a member to quote from newspaper reports and letters and the like if he wishes to adopt the opinions expressed therein as his own. Andrews: Mr. Pearson, how do you feel about a distinctive Canadian flag?

Andrews: What particular design do you have in mind?

This was on May 20, 1964. It goes on:
The eight, all editors, reporters or magazine writers, were shown into the newly decorated, gray-green living room where the Prime Minister relaxed with a scotch and soda, waiting to try his hand at "kite-flying" or, as some who attended the session called it later, "news management." Kiting a news story is a long-established political technique. Certain newspapermen are fed information from what they believe is a responsible source, and are encouraged to write it without attribution.
Government or party higher-ups then can judge public reaction and take this into account when they decide to go ahead or withdraw from the course they are considering.
The eight who had been summoned-Walter Stewart of the Toronto Star Weekly; Tim Creery and John Walker of Southams; Bob McKeown of Weekend; Ron Collister of the Telegram; Stan Westall of the Globe and Mail; Geoffrey Scott of CHCH-TV: Hamilton, and Chris Young, editor of the Ottawa Citizen-expected a flag discussion.

He said he was prepared to have the government stand or fall on the maple leaf flag.
The Prime Minister was careful, however, to make clear that the flag on the mantel was his personal choice.
Needless to say, with that kind of a kite in the air, the newspapermen lost no time, an hour and a half later, in rushing to their typewriters and giving the Prime Minister's views on the flag exactly as they heard them.
Despite the fact that two of the biggest news media-the Canadian Press and the C.B.C.-were not invited to 24 Sussex drive, the Prime Minister presumably got exactly what he was after: widespread debate on a specific flag design, for which he could not be held responsible.
That is the type and level of responsibility we have come to expect from the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the cabinet.
In the House of Commons next day, Prime Minister Pearson denied emphatically three times that any decision had been made by the government on the flag, and he was technically correct.
Most political reporters considered it came dangerously close to trying to shape the news that appeared in the newspapers, although the conference included representatives of some which opposed him on this issue.
But the Prime Minister certainly didn't distort his views, nor hold anything back to make the government look good. In fact, he said too much.
But next time he wants a kite flown, he'll likely allow someone just a little lower down to hold the string.
I think he needs a little more string to hold this kite.

But rather than attempt a compromise as to a time limit within which this committee must reach a decision, how about the committee's terms of reference including an instruction to report back within 30 days as to whether or not its members feel they will be able to reach a decision on the design?
If the committee members after 30 days of deliberation find that they cannot, or feel that they cannot reach accord by an 80 per cent majority, let us say-
I hear a chuckle over there. That is as much as the hon. member is prepared to give this suggestion. It might even be a giggle. But if members of the committee report back, in that interim report to the house, that they do not feel the matter can be decided by a majority, then back comes the issue into the house immediately without any more delay. This suggestion is a compromise and it is a compromise which will work. It is a compromise that will not prejudice any members either on the government side or on the opposition side.

However, if within that 30 days committee members find they are making progress and that there is every likelihood they will come to accord on a design, then the interim report will so disclose and they will be free then to return to their work and complete it, and make their final report to parliament, which would be subject only to limited debate, say, by the party leaders. In this way a great deal of time would be saved. This is the suggestion which should find at least sufficient merit in the minds of all members of the house to compel the party leaders to consider it.

But that is all we hear: They are going to give their decision when they vote. I would assure them that those who voted them in are liable to give their decision as well. We do not mind the silence on the other side and we rather enjoy these interjections. But I would like to see one hon. member opposite recognized and stand up on his feet. If he asks me a question, fine; I will try and answer it and if I cannot I will say so. If he wants to speak afterwards, then he can do so. But we enjoy their silence and I think the country does also. Their constituents must enjoy their silence and wonder where they stand. One can draw his own conclusions from their silence. Is it not an admission that they have nothing to say? Is it an admission that if they have anything to say they are afraid to say it. Of whom are they afraid, Mr. Speaker? I will tell you: They are afraid of their leader, the Prime Minister. If they are not afraid of their leader they are afraid to tell their constituents where they stand. I know every hon. member on the opposition side of the house who has taken part in this debate, and I know that I will stake my political future on what I say. I have to live with myself. I have to live with my principles and I have to live with my conscience; I cannot just sit on the fence. I should like to see some of the letters written by hon. members opposite to their constituents. They must be marked "Personal", "Confidential", and so on, but I expect we are going to come across a few. I

have heard rumours, but I do not want to base any argument on rumour.
Since the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Pickersgill) has once and for all spiked the argument that we are wasting time on this very important issue, let me say it is important to us that it be discussed, and that is why we feel it should be handed over to the people. I think the Prime Minister too must consider it a very important issue because he has shelved everything else, all the important legislation and promises hon. members opposite had made to the electorate of Canada. All this has been put aside and is gathering dust or has been put into cold storage because this present issue is an important matter. I realize that it is important and I have already told the house that I think it is important. The Acting Prime Minister said that the resolution is very important. While it contained the two flags it was most important; but fortunately the resolution was split in two, providing for one flag for our association with the British commonwealth of nations and the other for association-with what? With the ambitions of the Prime Minister.
I ask the government, or those who support this flag, to consider the question why they are afraid. Why do they not trust the Canadian people? Why do they not permit the Canadian people to have a voice in deciding the flag they want? We have quoted witness after witness from various organizations who have gone on record as saying they want a plebiscite. Why is the government afraid to submit this matter to a plebiscite? Why are they afraid to go to the people at the time of the next general election on this issue? Are they afraid of their decision? How can they be when I have heard some hon. members on the other side of the house give statistics to show that the three leaf flag carries a majority of support in Canada? In this case we who support the red ensign are in a minority. But, Mr. Speaker, even if the supporters of this new flag are in a majority, and even if they, the government, are in a majority in this house, thanks to that unholy alliance with certain splinter groups, has a majority the right to trample on the feelings or principles of a minority? If they have, then tell our French Canadian boys in Quebec-
We are defending the rights of minorities.

I am talking about holding
a plebiscite.
Canadian Flag

You are talking of
the red ensign.

I am saying that the plebiscite should decide; and if the hon. member wants to make a speech after I am finished then it is his privilege to get to his feet.
For the first three months, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister staked the life of his government on the decision on the flag he proposed. This hung like the sword of Damocles. A lot of those who were not supporters of the three leaf flag, being afraid of an election, got on the bandwagon and decided to support it.
Is that why some of your members are going to vote that way?
Mr. Speaker, I really think that if a member wants to ask a question he should receive your recognition by asking for it.
He does not answer.
The question was not properly asked.
He does not know the answer.

For three whole months the
sword of Damocles hung over us. I feel that the reason for this was that the Prime Minister was sure that if he did call an election he would win it. However, like the good politician he is he reads the press, not only those papers that flatter him but the others as well, and he must have read the article by Patrick Nicholson, a respected pressman, who wrote an article which appeared in the Quebec Chronicle of August 12. It was headlined "Election of flag could kill Liberals". The Prime Minister, having seen that, then withdrew his threat and said: "Boys, you can have a free vote as long as you leave me alone".
What Patrick Nicholson says, Mr. Speaker, is so interesting that I think it is worth while putting some of it on record. I have a lot of respect for the opinions of this man. He says:
The campaign strategists have been halted in their tracks-stunned.
I include in those campaign strategists, of course, the Prime Minister, as the chief strategist.
As most, but not all, Canadians know very well, parliament has long been stalled in its work largely because of "the flag issue". As the majority but by no means all, of Canadians are uneasily conscious, this is dividing the country-
This news must have disturbed the Prime Minister. The article then continues:

Canadian Flag
*-this is dividing the country even more disastrously than the stormiest issue recorded in our history books-the execution of the leader of the Metis revolt, Louis Riel, in 1885.
That is what Patrick Nicholson had to say. He then went on to state:
There is a parallel between Riel and the flag. The public uproar about the punishment of the chiefain of the French half breeds gravely divided Canada's two main ethnic groups, and changed the balance of federal politics for three quarters of a century.
The Prime Minister must have realized the situation and, as this article states-
-stepped in where Diefenbaker failed to tread.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest he did so because he could not foresee what this situation would do to this nation.
The article then refers to the French language newspaper, Le Droit, in which much has been said about this poll that was carried out. The article which I have been quoting continues as follows:
This poll discovered that a majority of Canadians, in every province except Quebec, prefer the Canadian ensign-
This is a long article and I do not intend to take up the time of the house to read it all, but Mr. Nicholson ends up by stating:
The significance of these figures, in the eyes of all Liberal strategists thinking in terms of an election-
Yes, an election is important.
-is that they clearly show that the flag issue would bring disastrous Liberal losses in nine provinces, and leave that party largely as the political arm of French Canada.
I suggest it was because the Prime Minister realized the situation as outlined by this article, rather than out of the goodness of his heart, that he freed his members taking the bit out of their mouths, allowing them a free vote. The Prime Minister became aware of these statements, which appeared in a great many more than one newspaper. I am sure that hon. gentleman is a politician to the extent he can appreciate the meaning of such statements.
. Mr. Speaker, since I spoke last on June 30, at the time the sword of Damocles hung over our heads when, if we had voted against the resolution, we would be forced out on the hustings, I have received a great number of letters and petitions. I do not intend to read the personal letters I have received, because of an impression I have that the Acting Prime Minister objects. I do however intend to read some representations made by organizations.
I received a petition from one Royal Canadian Legion branch in Elphinstone, Manitoba, [Mr. Mandziuk.j
which was signed by 50 members. This is not a large Legion branch, but I am sure if you check the names on this petition you will find that these members represent a great number of racial origins. We even have a few Indian veterans who are members of this Legion branch.
I intended to be generous to the Prime Minister in sending him a photostat copy of this petition, and like a gentleman he acknowledged receipt. Since his acknowledgement is not personal or confidential I hope hon. members will permit me to put it on record. The Prime Minister's letter is dated August 13, 1964, and is on the stationery of the office of the Prime Minister. The letter states:
The Prime Minister has asked me to acknowledge receipt of your letter of August 12 enclosing a copy of a petition that you received from the Royal Canadian Legion branch at Elphinstone, Manitoba, and to advise that he has noted it.
With kind regards.
Yours sincerely,-
I treasure the signature, Mr. Speaker. It is that of Jules Pelletier, secretary to the Prime Minister.
I received another letter from the Prime Minister's office, actually signed by his own hand. I received a telegram from the strongest Legion branch in my constituency, the branch in Minnedosa. I usually call this the capital of my riding. I received the telegram dated August 18 and, to be fair to the Prime Minister, thinking he would be interested to know that we were not just talking through our hats, as some hon. gentlemen opposite have suggested, I passed it on to him. He sent me this reply dated August 19, 1964:
Thank you for your letter of August 14 enclosing the telegram that you received from the Minnedosa branch of the Royal Canadian Legion, advising that the branch membership supports the red ensign as Canada's official flag, and which I have noted.
Apparently the Prime Minister decided that valour was the better part of policy and retreated, deciding to give a free vote. The vote has always been free as far as we are concerned, in spite of what the Acting Prime Minister has suggested.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that any party that does not listen to the opinion of the grassroots cannot know what is taking place and will lose out in the end. I have attempted to keep in touch with the grassroots in my constituency to find out how these people feel about putting this issue to a plebiscite or referendum. I have written many letters to my constituents, although without the same

influence as bumper stickers have, financed by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis), or those large buttons, of which I have seen little in the past months.
A small weekly newspaper in my constituency, the Gazette Reporter of Rivers, Manitoba, published an article under the heading "Flag Fight". Rivers, Manitoba, is in an area very close to C.G.A.T.C., which is the largest air training centre in western Canada. This newspaper is read by a great number of people in this area who cannot express themselves because they belong to Her Majesty's armed forces. This newspaper is published by Mr. Larry Bell. During the past four elections I have attempted to find out which political party he supports, but to no avail. He always greets me pleasantly but refuses to disclose his affiliation. He stated this in his editorial dated July 16, 1964:
A writer in the Toronto Star waxes exuberant in describing Prime Minister Pearson's handling of the "flag issue."
As that T.V. star, Hazel, would say when something of excitement takes place: "This is a doozie". The article continues:
Recalling how the great Mongol conqueror, Genghis Khan, stormed out of the east in 1215 waving a banner of nine yak tails, he pictures Pearson similarly storming out of Ottawa in 1964 holding aloft his gonfalon of conjoined maple leaves.
The most remarkable thing about the Big Flag Fight (says the writer) has been the transformation of Mr. Pearson from a mild, diplomatic, even hesitant leader to a purposeful commander, storming the bastions of public opinion with a new battle banner and a strident cry of "Excelsior!"
Somehow, other news media reports and comment just don't back up the picture. Pussy-footing, cat-and-mouse tactics, backing and sidling-all duly headlined in the public prints-have overtook the original "Excelsior", marred its brightness. In any event, it is to be hoped "Mike" doesn't meet the same fate as that cryer and his banner with the strange device.
I think that is a masterful editorial which reflects accurately the thought of the people in respect of the tactics used by the Prime Minister and those who support him in trying to hoist this flag on the Canadian people. In a close circle of friends let us do it with as little debate as possible-that is what the Prime Minister hoped. The less the people know about it the better it is for us, because they only campaigned on the flag issue when it pleased their fancy, where they figured they were on safe ground. They did not dare to mention the flag in my constituency, I assure you. I never heard it mentioned during the last two election campaigns or before that.
Here is an anonymous poem which appeared in the Hamiota Echo which is pub-

lished by one, Fred Venables. I must admit he is a supporter of mine but I do not think that was the reason for publishing the poem. He is not a poet so it must have been written by someone else. It is a real masterpiece. It is titled "Freedom of Choice" and reads as follows:
Little boy blue come blow your horn,
Your flag's in the making, an era is born.
What matters the people you swore you would serve.
Just show them you still have an unholy nerve.
You know that the ensign is loved by us all,
Especially those who answered the call.
We fought and we died for the old union jack.
And wherever it took us we never looked back.
Those flags bravely flutter all over our land,
From ocean to ocean, and many a strand.
From Arctic's cold shore to the southernmost seas,
They proudly unfold themselves in the breeze...
But you L. B. P. think you know what is best.
You've made up your mind so to heck with the rest.
But let us remind you just what is at stake.
We don't give up easy for something we hate.
You look to the people to keep you in power,
But your own lack of judgment turns everything sour.
You dream of your three maple leaves on a
stick.
No wonder you've edged it with blue, good and thick.
It is a rather long poem and I know some people do not appreciate good poetry. I say that because I see they are talking among themselves, but I will give copies to those who really want to read the whole poem.

It does not rhyme. I can say that much to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The poem ends this way:
We know you are badgered but never say die.
There are things in the offing that will make it quite clear,
You can't fool with people nor what they hold dear.
And if you are wise you will draw in your horns,
And go to the people as you should have done.
Our freedom of choice that we fought to retain,
We have it before, we can do it again.
You know now what the threat consists of, Mr. Speaker. I think this poem written in August gives a clear indication that the propaganda of stamps, bumper stickers and press releases which wasted the time of the house has not caught fire in any part of Canada to any extent. If it were not for the remarks of the Acting Prime Minister I might read two short letters, but perhaps I will anyway. They are very short. One reads:

Canadian Flag
I hope you will do all you can to save the red ensign.
The letter is signed and if you want the name I will give it. It is a beautiful girl.
Give it.

You are married. I do not think I should. I have another one which reads:
T am in favour of keeping our Canadian red ensign flag.
I could bring dozens and dozens before the house. Today's Ottawa Citizen has a very interesting headline, "Pearson Can't Escape Flag". That is interesting. Here is what the article says in part:
-in a city which has decked itself in hundreds of red ensigns and union jacks-in about equal numbers-for the confederation centenary celebrations. Even the Maple Leaf bakery flies the red ensign here.
Where is that?
Charlottetown. That is in today's Ottawa Citizen, and it is very interesting.	-
Order.
Is somebody out of order?
You are.

We have heard nothing but "order, order, order", "question, question, question", "carried, carried, carried". We have heard nothing else during the last 12 days of debate. I have told you the reason why and you can guess the rest. I want to refer the house to an editorial in the Telegram, a Toronto paper-good old Toronto. It appeared in the issue of August 22 last. Apparently the Telegram is not sick and tired of our obstruction.
We are.

You see, there is another member who is glued to his seat. I sympathize with him. I know that the tongues of many on that side are aching because they want to get up and say something, but an order is an order and the discipline of an army must be obeyed.

speechtext: Is the hon. member rising on a question of privilege?

If the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) had attended more regularly the house sittings he would know that I have delivered a speech on the

amendment and the subamendment now under consideration.

It must have been all right, Mr. Speaker, because some members applauded but this device does not work and I did not catch a word. If the hon. member would care to repeat it after I am finished I would appreciate it. All I can do is blame the government.
It has not worked for six months.

I was about to refer to an editorial in the Telegram headed "Ask the People". I am only going to quote a few sentences. It starts by saying:
The Canadian ensign must not be lowered without the consent of the people.
That is what we have been trying to tell the house for the last 17 or 18 days that we have been debating this matter. It must not be done without the consent of the people. If a majority of the people prefer to have the three leaves I will be the first one to salute the new flag, because a law is a law. We are a civilized nation. I quote further:
No decision of the House of Commons, by free vote or otherwise, to strike our historic ensign and replace it with a pennant of the Prime Minister's choosing can be construed as expressing the consensus of the nation.
Those who are pushing the new flag, Mr. Speaker, did not even receive a majority of the votes in the last election. They do not have a mandate any more than we have. The editorial goes on to say that certain legislative programs are introduced by the government and the government takes its responsibility for its plans and policies. Then the editorial continues:
But the flag issue is different. Here is a matter that touches the hearts, the emotions, the loyalties of virtually all Canadians. A parliamentary vote that would destroy the country's flag would leave deep and festering scars for years to come. It is far too important to be settled by parliamentary compromise.
Even if a compromise were arrived at by members of parliament I feel that it should be put to the people in a plebiscite or some other way to find out whether they accept that compromise. I read further:
There was no suggestion that parliament would be presented with a single, peculiar pennant design and be told that this must be our flag. If there had been such a proposition, it is quite possible that Mr. Pearson's minority representation in the House of Commons would have been considerably smaller.

At the outset of my remarks I should like to draw to the attention of this house a gross exaggeration which appeared in the Toronto daily Star last Friday to the effect that this debate had cost the Dominion of Canada half a billion dollars up to that date. I hope the Star corrects this mistake. Even if one accepts its own figure of $33,000 a day as the cost of running the House of Commons and multiplies it by the number of days we have been sitting on this issue, it becomes apparent how far from accuracy this figure really is.
My first observations will be on the subject of the government's proposed flag. The weak position of the proposed three maple leaf flag has been revealed by the lack of support from the government benches. If government members were enthusiastic about it and were sure of their constituents' backing I would think they would be on their feet speaking of its merits and advantages. They have passed up many opportunities to tell this house and the country why they prefer the three maple leaf flag and why they think the Canadian red ensign should be pulled down and discarded. Some of them have expressed their opinions fluently and I will make reference to these deliberations later.
I would like to dwell for a few minutes on incidents that indicate further the weak position of the three leaf flag. We are all aware of the many and varied schemes which were used to no avail to promote this flag. When it appears on cars it is now a sad spectacle-it has become a tattle-tale gray. Much of the promotion must surely have been embarrassing to the Prime Minister, especially when one of his ministers lowered this flag to the position of a bumper sticker. This three leaf flag has taken a terrific slide-from the top of a pole in front of the parliament buildings to a bumper sticker, which is just about as low as it can get. Indications coming in from across the country verify that its popularity and support have slipped about the same degree in the opinion of the vast majority of our people.
Surely by now, after this vain effort to break the will of the Canadian people, the Prime Minister will get his political ship 20220-478
Canadian Flag
back on course and go along with the wishes of the majority by allowing a plebiscite.
Some of his backbenchers have seen the handwriting on the wall and have so expressed themselves. On August 19 the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) said:
We on this side have wondered how it is that so many people in Canada are staunchly entrenched behind the red ensign, a fact we did not expect: people who would otherwise have fondly and readily welcomed a new distinctive flag.
There are many reasons for this attitude and reasons why it is gaining strength with each passing day.
Many people across Canada did not take the Prime Minister seriously when he talked of adopting a distinctive flag for Canada. This is so, first, because many of the government promises still remain promises or died within the 60 days of decision. Second, others fully believed that the new flag would be a modification of the red ensign. Of course, when the three leaf flag design was given its back door introduction the props were knocked from under this line of thought. It was then and there that the backers of the Canadian red ensign took their stand. Their ranks were substantially increased when the Prime Minister announced the method by which he hoped to force his flag on this nation. More people took up the fight from resentment of the brainwashing methods by which he hoped to influence opinion in support of his three leaf flag.
Now, referring again to the observations of the hon. member from York East, I can assure him I am in full accord with the last statement of his speech when he said: "so that we may give the Canadian flag back to the people to whom it belongs". This is all we are asking. Give the people of Canada the flag of their choice. This problem can be settled just as easily as that, by way of a plebiscite.
There are many reasons why the three leaf design did not catch on as anticipated by the Prime Minister. One need only look at it to realize it lacked anything that would create enthusiasm. It is destitute of magnetism which would encourage the people to rally around and give support. It is too bad the Prime Minister had not taken heed of these words of Henry Ward Beecher:
A thoughtful mind, when it sees a nation's flag, sees not the flag only, but the nation itself; and whatever may be its symbols, its insignia, he reads chiefly in the flag the government, the principles, the truths, the history which belongs to the nation that sets it forth.

Canadian Flag
The three leaf flag does not embody these things which are essential.
We need only read the speech of the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) when he spoke on August 24 as reported at page 7178 of Hansard to find more reasons for the failure to create any fervour for the three leaf flag. Some of the hon. member's statements have been refuted in the press by a letter signed by six of his colleagues, but to my knowledge only one of those six has spoken in this debate, and that member, when he made his speech just a little later the same day, did not contradict any of the statements made by the hon. member from York-Humber. So we must believe the statement made by the hon. member for York-Humber when he told us that the government caucus had no voice in the decision on the three leaf flag. There must have been very good reasons for keeping Liberal members excluded from information so vital to the government and to the country. This is the usual procedure for all conspiracy. Here was the beginning of the disunity which has now fanned out across this nation.
The introduction of the three leaf flag was no doubt as shocking to supporters of the government as it was to millions of Canadians, particularly to those Canadians living in constituencies where the flag was given the silent treatment during the election campaign and where they were told there were so many other goodies in store for them. After the silent treatment given government members prior to the introduction of his personal flag there must surely have been much quiet, as well as open, resentment when the three leaf flag appeared on the scene. Handcuffed as they were from the start, the government members on hearing the resolution read, at once realized they were still shackled because they could not speak out against the two top men of their party-the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau)-unless they had a lot of intestinal fortitude. The die was cast. They had no voice, so very few of them have spoken.
Now I ask this house, could anyone expect the Canadian people to accept this three leaf flag with open arms, conceived as it was in secrecy by a few individuals; introduced to the house like a cold clam with no history or tradition; and since that time promoted by ways and means that did nothing more than build up more resistance to its approval?
Furthermore, much information has been brought to the surface during this debate which has had a telling effect across the

country. Many people are giving the matter a second look and have come to realize that a flag given approval at this time will be the flag as long as we stand as a nation. I would venture to say that if the Prime Minister had unfurled this three leaf flag during the election campaign he would have saved Canada this present embarrassment because he would not have had the opportunity to form a government.
My constituents are asking me, "If the government forces this flag on the country, who will fly it?" This is a good question and I would think the only place we could be sure of having it flown would be on federal property. Also, I find much opposition to the two flag idea. A flag we are not ashamed of in any company should be our flag, and that flag is the Canadian red ensign, which to this date has never failed to rally support in peace or war, and we will not fail it now. We want one country and one flag.
I will at this time quote from an editorial from the Owen Sound Sun-Times of May 25, 1964 headed, "Will Quebec fly New Flag?" It reads:
Midst all the turmoil over the "new Canadian flag" there can be no more moot question (nor uncertain one) than whether a new standard for the nation will bring about greater or lesser unity. And of topmost importance in this regard must be the ultimate results on relations between French Canadian Quebec and the rest of Canada.
Will, for instance, the people of Quebec accept Prime Minister Pearson's new flag as their national standard? Or will the Quebec flag, in several forms but always exclusively featuring the fleur-de-lis, continue to be flown throughout that province, along with the tricolour of France, but seldom, if ever, Canada's present colours?
Unless Quebec accepts as its own any new flag Mr. Pearson may have parliament approve, then all the Prime Minister's efforts are in vain. He will have failed to promote that unity so vitally needed for the continued progress of this young nation. In fact, it may well be that disunity has been promoted. The hard core at least of the Canadian Legion is not likely to easily give up their support of the red ensign which has come to mean so much to them as they have served their nation. Nor, if the new flag is an unprofitable compromise to Canadians of French ancestry, will it be viewed kindly by other provinces which see themselves as distinctively important to Canada as a whole as in Quebec.
We have heard members opposite say we should forget our past and our history, which is embodied in the red ensign. They say that it is insignificant and would be better forgotten. Now, it is most difficult to accept this sort of thinking because, as individuals our own past can mean so much to us. When one applies for an important position, his past record is very thoroughly investigated, and

rightly so. It is usually, if I may use another example, the deciding factor when an investor is speculating on which company or corporation he will invest in. If he is a wise investor he examines closely the record of the president and the directors of the organization. He looks into the financial statement and all the past history of the said company before investing. The same principle applies to any nation. Many decisions made by its own people and other countries are based on that country's past performance or its history. We cannot ignore history or wash it out. Some may distort it, but we can never obliterate it.
Therefore, it is just nonsense to say that the history and tradition in which the Canadian red ensign is involved and so interwoven should be forgotten. If we are to believe this, the prospects for our future have reached an all-time low. It would be a sad day for this nation if we were to sit idly by and let this calamity overtake us. We cannot let our people down. We will continue to fight until a suitable solution is presented or until it is agreed to let the Canadian people decide.
I quote from this short editorial from the Sudbury Star because it is relevant:
Quebec is only one province in the dominion of Canada. But it elects 75 members to the 265 member House of Commons. The Liberal government is a minority government. It has only 128 members in the Commons of which 46 come from Quebec. Without the support of that province the Liberals could not form a government-and this has been demonstrated time and time again in Canada's political history.
The Liberals need Quebec and Quebec needs the Liberals. Politically, it is as simple as that. Behind all the high-sounding platitudes about "rights" and "unity" can be found hard-faced politics where power and the retention of power are the rewards.
Canadians might ask themselves if there is any other country in the world where a minority group dictates to the majority to the same extent? Or where a government bends over backwards to please the minority and tries to convince the majority that they should agree to domination by the minority. That is what is happening in Canada today.
Mr. Speaker, the brunt of the attack in this flag debate has fallen on the shoulders of one man. That man is the Prime Minister of this country. Perhaps this is justified as he has made statements indicating his willingness to take the responsibility. We know he had the help of two or three people in selecting the three leaf design. We know he promoted it by way of a press release to a selected group of news reporters. We know he took it upon himself to make an appeal to the Canadian Legion rally in Winnipeg. In fact he has played the leading part 20220-478J
Canadian Flag
in the act, but I am convinced that he has taken some direction from his braintrust on some of the methods used in trying to sell it to the Canadian people.
The Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) made his contribution by way of bumper stickers. The Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) made sure of good coverage with the three leaf postage stamp. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) broke the sad story to the Queen. Other ministers no doubt took a hand in the regrettable incident which has upset Canadian people more than anything in our history, outside of war itself.
The Prime Minister has shown good judgment on many occasions in the past during his years as a diplomat. He has been honoured many times. He has commanded much respect on numerous occasions. If I may, I will cite a recent event, a report of which makes special reference to him. This is an excerpt taken from a report in the Ottawa Journal of July 16 on the commonwealth conference held recently in London:
Pearson emerged-in the opinion of observers from Australia to Zanzibar-as one of the most effective participants in this conference. His experience in commonwealth and empire meetings goes back to the 1930's.
His speech Monday was regarded as a turning point on the Rhodesian issue when-as representative of the senior white dominion-he put forward his declaration on racial equality and called for release of political prisoners in the African colony.
Right now a great opportunity is being presented to him, whereby he can render a great service to his country. He can play the leading role in a new act with every Canadian playing a part. He can settle this flag turmoil quietly and to the satisfaction of the majority by letting the Canadian people select their flag. It is the only way he can settle the issue and keep the high respect of his fellow Canadians. He must surely see the folly of following the course leading to disunity. We know, Mr. Speaker, he is exposed to great pressure from within his party by people who do not fully realize what the consequences will be if the three maple leaf flag is forced on this nation.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) must surely realize that he would not have the support of the communists and many known radicals on this issue if he were acting in the best interests of this nation. I implore him to free himself of these millstones which threaten to strangle him and, in the interests of unity, assume the role of a free thinking prime minister who will not be intimidated

Finally I said, "This debate on the flag has turned out to be a tough nut to crack". He replied, "We must reach an agreement; we must compromise"; and, of course, I agree with him. I think this is the attitude of a good many members on the other side of the chamber, which they would express if they had the opportunity to do so.
It is not necessary, Mr. Speaker, that I speak at any length in defence of the Canadian red ensign. It is becoming more respected, more loved, and is flown by more Canadians right across this country, including those in the province of Quebec, with every passing day. On a recent visit to Montreal I saw more Canadian red ensigns flying than at any time over the years. Speaking of the French, Mr. Speaker, I noticed a newspaper write-up recently about a young Canadian by the name of Joseph Cote, who by his name, I assume is French. The report spoke of an extended hitch-hiking trip which this young university history student took through Europe, Africa and Asia lasting over 300 days. To make sure he would be properly appreciated and recognized, he wore the

Canadian red ensign on the outside of his packsack.
Was he from Quebec?

Well, the name would indicate that he was. I would also like to say that I stood in front of the United Nations building in New York with some American friends, and there in front of that impressive building flew the flags of all member nations. The Canadian red ensign stood out among those flags and I was proud to point to it and say, "There flies our Canadian flag". I have another quote here from our daily paper, Mr. Speaker. I understand that it claims to be independent, and I know this is the case because they have never given me any favours. This article says:
We Favour the Red Ensign
The Sun-Times makes a very honest, and we believe successful effort, to be independent in our political viewpoint. Helpful in this regard is the fact that staff members connected with opinion voiced are quite diversified in the political field, including those who honestly attempt to remain free of party bias of any kind because of the paper's policy of independence.
We view the flag issue as most unfortunate at this time, as has been pointed out in these columns previously. Nor is it an issue that should bring on an election, if Mr. Pearson has such a thought, as has been suggested.
The Sun-Times editorially favours the red ensign, a flag of which Canadians of all ancestral background can be proud in that it has been bom out of the experience of a young, aggressive and farsighted nation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that regardless of what happens as a result of this debate, I predict that the red ensign or a compromise of that flag will fly over Canada long after our time.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great feeling of pride and a deep sense of responsibility that I rise to take part in this historic and important debate. In doing so I would like to take this opportunity of bringing to the attention of the house the views of constituents whom I am honoured to represent, as well as some views of my own. At the outset I should like to state that I am not only quite satisfied with the flag that is universally acknowledged and accepted as Canada's flag, the red ensign, but I am strongly in support of its retention.
Constituents of mine with whom I have discussed this matter, as well as the numerous ones who have taken time out to send me their views in letters, have with one exception indicated in no uncertain terms that they

also wish to see the retention of the Canadian red ensign. Knowing them as I do, however, and being aware of their keen interest in the all important matter of Canadian unity, I feel quite certain that they would be more than willing to accept some variation of the present flag if it were felt desirable by a majority of the people of Canada. But, Mr. Speaker, I am also quite certain that the great majority of them would insist that in any new flag which may be decided upon there should be some recognition of our two founding races.
After those brief observations I should like to deal with one particular aspect which has come to the forefront not only of this debate but during the past few years when certain people in many parts of Canada have talked over the possibility of a new flag. The point I should like to deal with at this time is the emphasis which has been placed by most speakers in this house on a distinctive Canadian flag. The speakers who have preceded me have dwelt upon this point. Some have referred to the definitions of the word "distinctive" which are found in various dictionaries. Therefore, like many other hon. members I have been quite interested to try to get to the bottom of this idea of a distinctive Canadian flag, and I have found from looking through various dictionaries that the definitions show little variation. In the latest dictionary I consulted I noticed that "distinctive" is defined as "marking or expressing distinction". When I looked up the meaning of "distinction" in the same dictionary I found three definitions were given. The first variation was "an act of distinguishing a difference or differences"; the second one was "a difference"; and the third "a distinguishing quality or mark".
After looking at the red ensign flying above the peace tower, atop public buildings across Canada and many private dwellings, I would defy anyone to convince me from the definitions in the dictionary of the two words "distinctive" and "distinction" that our present red ensign is not a distinctive flag. Be that as it may, I will return to the subject I mentioned a while ago and say that I am sure that the constituents in my area would be more than willing to compromise on some variation of our present flag in respect to the all important subject of the unity of our nation. Before going further let me say that, despite the speeches we have heard in this flag debate, and no matter how long it goes on, I hope all of us realize that the unity of our country is by far the most important fact.

Before giving the house any further views on the red ensign or the possibility of coming to some agreement on an acceptable alternate design, I should like to deal briefly with some of the points which have come out in the debate so far, as well as some of the charges which have been made in the articles which have appeared in various newspapers and in statements made on television. First of all, I should like to say a few words regarding the charge, which I say is unfounded and unjustified, that the official opposition is obstructing the business of this house. Many speakers have mentioned this and many of our newsmen have given their version as to what has been going on during these last two or three weeks. I have been very interested in one or two of these observations.
Another charge which has been made is that we are filibustering. In this respect 1 should like to mention the speech delivered in this house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp). In his speech he roamed the field far and wide, and I noticed that on seven or eight occasions, while looking up to the ceiling and possibly bowing to any members of the fourth estate who might be within his vision, he mentioned the word "filibuster".
How many days ago was that?
That was a few days ago.
Then it is not a filibuster.

Well, let us take a look at some of the observations from our worldly wise newsmen. I would like to quote an article which apeared in the Toronto Star on August 31, which is not too long ago, from the pen of Mr. Peter Newman. In reference to the unfounded reports of the obstruction of parliament he stated:
The Liberal administration, unaccountably, has no major bills ready for debate.
Hon. members opposite may say "So what?" They may ask: "Who is this gentleman to say that we have no legislation ready for parliament?" I recall when he penned a recent fictional edition for them, at which time he was considered the fountain of knowledge; but somehow or other when he talks in this way they seem to want to turn off the water.
I do not think by any means we need to stop at Mr. Newman's observations, because here is another one on Preview Commentary by Mr. Blair Fraser under date of August 20. He stated:

People are getting so bored with the flag debate, and so cynical about it, that it seems to me we're beginning to accept as facts a number of things that aren't true.
One is the charge that the Progressive Conservatives are blocking the business of government by their filibuster on the flag resolution. This is not true. Parliament has got through all the work that the Prime Minister stipulated must be done before the house could adjourn for a summer recess, with the lone exception of the flag resolution; if the resolution were brought to a vote tomorrow, parliament would adjourn and probably wouldn't come back until October. The only thing that's being held up by the filibuster is a holiday ..or the tired M.P.'s-a holiday and a chance to get back to their ridings and attend to the useful work they do there.
Another charge that I don't believe to be true is that the Conservative campaign against the .maple leaf flag is a mere political ploy, just a device to force an early election on an issue they think they could win on-or, alternatively, that the Liberal determination to have the maple leaf flag is no more than a piece of electoral strategy for the recapture of Quebec. This cynical view has no factual support that I know of. I don't know any reason to doubt that the people who have spoken are saying what they really believe, and furthermore that they think they're speaking for their electors.
This is the man who has seldom if ever lauded the work of the Conservative party. I can only say that it is possible his recent trip through the beautiful country of Churchill constituency, which he made by canoe, gave him for once in his life a much clearer picture of the situation. We have also heard this charge made by other people.
I will conclude my remarks in respect of this subject >
by saying ;that in my capacity during the last few days as acting whip I can unequivocally state that in the main our members are extremely desirous of speaking during this debate. Many of them have told me that they have been unable to place all their views before this house in the allotted time. In answer to some of the criticisms directed toward some members on this side who'have spoken twice during the debate, I should state that many have said they have hot used their allotted 40 minutes and wish to put further statements on the record. Many others who have not spoken as yet have not spoken because they have given way to other members who wished to speak on a specific date. I suggest that the charges of obstruction are false, and charges of filibuster can only be taken for what they are apparently worth.
Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to enter this debate and I can state here and now there are other members Who still wish to speak, probably at some length.

I also wish to deal briefly with some of the remarks made today by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). He followed the lead of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) and took part in an unwarranted attack on the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). It might be of interest to note, for the benefit of those members not present at that time, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce took part in an unwarranted attack on the Leader of the Opposition, until that right hon. gentleman entered this chamber, and then completely changed his speech and said no more in that vein. That performance can only be compared to children in primary school, grade five or six, who fall silent when a teacher who has been absent for some time returns to the room. The tune certainly does change.
Mr. Speaker, as far as the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate are concerned, I should like to say that I am in disagreement. That hon. minister referred to the 1940's in an attempt to suggest that the Tories did not support the red ensign. Having read that committee report I understand the official vote was 23 to 1, and there were several Tory members on that committee. That committee was established to study and recommend a Canadian flag.
The Minister of Transport made one statement with which I am m agreement. He said he was a stupid Anglo-Saxon. I agree with him, of course, if he is speaking only for himself.

That was certainly not my intention, and I am sure the minister was speaking for himself.
Mr. Speaker, having talked with a great number of people I am convinced that many Canadians are perturbed about the way this flag issue has been brought before parliament. Many members have made this statement before during this debate, and it hardly needs repeating. However if the government is not aware of the situation as yet, I should like to say on behalf of my constituents that they are strongly in support of retaining the red ensign as Canada's flag. They also feel that any change in the Canadian flag involves far more than the presentation by government of a resolution, such as is before this house, followed by a vote by members of parliament, which in all likelihood will be in acceptance of a proposed national flag which will re-

main as such for more than 100 years. These people certainly disagree with that procedure.
Mr. Speaker, I have mentioned that I personally support with vigour the Canadian red ensign, as do the people I represent. During the course of this debate many speakers have mentioned some of the history behind the red ensign. I have a few notes here I should like to refer to in an attempt to illustrate why my constituents support retention of the red ensign. It is true that the Canadian red ensign is in grave danger of being discarded as Canada's national flag. That danger is intensified by the lack of knowledge on the part of a great many Canadians who know nothing of the historic symbols and tradition. Recorded history actually contradicts many of the things people take for granted about the red ensign. Past generations of Canadians have asked for and proudly adopted the red ensign. They used it in defiance of restraining orders. Today, sanctified by the blood of our fighting forces, steeped in our traditions, the red ensign by common acceptance and long usage has become known to every nation and country as Canada's flag. Despite all the evidence of common approval, the Prime Minister has stated that he fully intends to write the obituary of the red ensign as Canada's identifying flag.
We all know that by order in council No. 5888, dated September 15, 1945, the red ensign was declared Canada's distinctive flag. It was adopted at that time because Canada's history has been established under that flag, and there was then no question in respect of its worthiness. Why are we now faced with this sudden reappraisal in 1964?
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note about the history of the red ensign that one pamphlet published by the Canadian Legion which, as is well known, is an extremely strong supporter of this flag, contained the following very interesting observations. This is a very interesting observation.
General H. D. G. Crerar, the distinguished commander of the first Canadian army in world war II, recorded an incident of great historical significance for all Canadians when, recounting an official welcome to him in Ottawa on August 8, 1945, by our wartime prime minister, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, he wrote in the March, 1963 issue of The Legionary:
"As we moved away from the central entrance of the parliament buildings, Mr. King turned sideways in the car and looked upwards to the peace tower where, at the top, the Canadian red ensign waved. He then said, 'And that. General, is another problem which your Canadian army has
Canadian Flag
solved for Canada-the matter of our national flag.' "
Little did he know at that time that this debate would be taking place in this year 1964. To get back to some of the history of the ensign, we find that ignorance of the Canadian flag is alarmingly prevalent and it begets misunderstanding, prejudice and bigotry. These are all weapons in the arsenal of the proponents of a new flag. This lack of knowledge is not confined to the man in the street. It is found at all levels. Some school children and school teachers know little or nothing about the flag. When it is explained to them they are amazed. Why is not this information made public, they ask. They are susceptible to the clamour for a new flag only because they are uninformed about the old one.
The trouble is that our flag suffers from underexposure in our country. Poor publicity and indifference are responsible for this. Anyone interested can find an abundance of historical and pictorial material showing use of the red ensign in Canada long before confederation. It came here with Prince Rupert and the Company of Adventurers trading into Hudson's bay. The archives of the Hudson's Bay Company have numerous references to the flag from 1670 on.
The Hudson's Bay Company was not a mere trading company. It was the government of that day. It controlled trade, settlement and the building of forts. It armed ships and soldiers, passed and enforced laws and punished offenders. Its powers could scarcely have been more sweeping. For two centuries a large part of what is now Canada was governed under the company's charter and flag.
Canada holds the west today because she fell heir to the achievements of the Hudson's Bay Company and the Nor'westers with whom they united in 1821. All that area drained by the rivers flowing into Hudson's bay was controlled by the company until Canada formed a dominion capable of taking it over. The flag of that company was the red ensign.
This is just a little of the history of the flag which of late has been in danger of being removed as Canada's national flag. There are many other points of view I should like to bring before the house at this time, but I see my time is getting on. As many speakers today have said, I think we should endeavour to arrive at some means of settling this issue, and several means have been suggested. I have mentioned the views of my constituents and my own personal views in relation to the
